# Suppression of spiral density waves in collisionless accretion flows

**Authors:** Stephen Majeski Matthew W. Kunz ††thanks: E-mail: stephen.majeski@colorado.edu Affiliation: JILA, University of Colorado and National Institute of Standards and Technology, 440 UCB, Boulder, CO 80309-0440, USA Jason Dexter Affiliation: JILA, University of Colorado and National Institute of Standards and Technology, 440 UCB, Boulder, CO 80309-0440, USA Affiliation: Department of Astrophysical Sciences, Princeton University, Peyton Hall, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Affiliation: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, PO Box 451, Princeton, NJ 08543, USA Affiliation: Department of Astrophysical and Planetary Sciences, University of Colorado, 391 UCB, Boulder, CO 80309-0391, USA

## Abstract

Spiral density waves are ubiquitous phenomena in differentially rotating flows. They are non-modal, non-axisymmetric perturbations that, due to shear in the background flow, possess time-evolving wavenumbers, frequencies, and amplitudes. In global simulations of optically thin, low-luminosity black-hole accretion flows, the excitation of such waves leads to spiral patterns in the plasma density that influence the morphology of the emission region. As such, the observed variabilities of such accretion flows are expected to be affected by the behavior of spiral density waves. Thus far, investigations of spiral density waves in accretion flows have exclusively used the assumption that the accretion-flow plasmas are in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) at all times. In reality, hot and diffuse accretion-flow plasmas are expected to deviate far from LTE, and should be modeled accordingly. Here, we employ a combination of kinetic and fluid models to describe spiral density wave propagation, damping, and excitation in a collisionless shearing sheet, which more accurately represents the plasma conditions of low-luminosity accretion flows than do models that assume LTE. We find that micro-physical plasma instabilities are especially important in determining how spiral density waves behave, because the weak particle scattering that they induce leads to appreciable viscous damping. Observational implications of these results include reduced emission-region variability, which may improve agreement between Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) observations and simulation/theory, as well as a reduction in emission-region pattern speeds compared to simulations employing LTE, which bears on the interpretation of eventual EHT movies.

#### Keywords:

## 1 Introduction

Non-axisymmetric spiral density waves are a common occurrence in differentially rotating flows. Well-documented examples range from spiral arms in galaxies, to perturbations driven by forming planets in protoplanetary disks, and even to waves in planetary rings (Lin & Shu, 1964; Pérez et al., 2016; Goldreich & Tremaine, 1978, see, e.g.,). Such waves are also anticipated to arise in accretion flows around the supermassive black holes of galactic nuclei (Jiang et al., 2019; Secunda et al., 2019; Conroy et al., 2023; Brown & Ogilvie, 2026, e.g.,), although observations have yet to achieve the resolution needed to detect them directly. Their existence there has been predicted primarily using magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation and theory: by global, general-relativistic calculations (EHT et al., 2022b) as well as local, non-relativistic ones (Heinemann & Papaloizou, 2009a, e.g., the shearing box;). Both find the excitation of spiral density waves when the accretion flow is turbulent (Heinemann & Papaloizou, 2009b; Fromang et al., 2007; Ross & Latter, 2018, e.g.,). Turbulence, in turn, has long been known to arise naturally from a host of instabilities that extract free energy from the shear of the rotating flow, the best known being the magnetorotational instability (Balbus & Hawley, 1991; Hawley & Balbus, 1991, MRI,). The MRI requires little more than a weakly magnetized plasma orbiting with an angular velocity that decreases outwards—conditions generic to nearly every class of accretion flow—and so both it and the turbulence it drives in its nonlinear phase are expected to be widespread. By association, spiral density waves should be just as prevalent.

Recent work has brought the observational imprint of these waves into focus for black-hole accretion flows. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration compiled an immense library of global GRMHD simulations designed to replicate the observed near-horizon emission from the accretion flow onto the black hole at the center of our galaxy, Sgr A∗ (EHT et al., 2022b). In virtually all of the simulated emission scenarios, spiral patterns were the dominant non-axisymmetric component of the synchrotron emission, indicating the presence of spiral density waves that had been excited farther out in the flow and propagated inwards. As discussed by Conroy et al. (2025), this presents a unique opportunity: through these waves, the morphology and variability of emission in the region very near the black-hole event horizon may be directly connected to conditions farther out in the flow. Such a connection is especially valuable in light of the so-called “variability crisis”: the fiducial models of the EHT library, as a whole, overestimated the variability of Sgr A∗, and any individual models that did not overestimate the variability were instead unable to satisfy other observational constraints. If spiral density waves are a significant contributor to that variability, the discrepancy implicates the modeling of the outer regions in which the waves are excited, rather than that of the near-horizon region where the emission is produced. This paper takes up that possibility by relaxing an assumption common to previous work—that the plasma is in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE)—an assumption with little justification in the hot and dilute plasmas of low-luminosity accretion flows, such as those around M87∗ and Sgr A∗. We posit that departures from LTE—driven by both the spiral density waves and the turbulence that excites them—modify the inward propagation of these waves, thereby linking the non-equilibrium thermodynamics of accretion flows to their observed properties and offering a potential route toward resolving the variability crisis of Sgr A∗.

### 1.1 Spiral Wave Excitation in MRI Turbulence

Before considering how non-LTE effects may change spiral density waves, it is instructive to review first the mechanism that excites them. Although we focus solely on accretion flows in this work, the underlying physics of spontaneous density wave excitation actually does not require rotation at all. Instead, the essential ingredients are flow shear and fluctuations in the fluid vorticity. First described by Chagelishvili et al. (1997), the basic process for density wave excitation in sheared flows is as follows (see figure 1). Initially, an aperiodic fluctuation in the fluid vorticity, known as a vortical wave, must be present. When strongly misaligned with the sheared flow, these waves perturb the density very weakly, thus, the initial conditions are nearly free of density perturbations. This vortical wave must also be “leading”, which means that the ratio of its wavevector components perpendicular and parallel to the background flow $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}$ has the same sign as the gradient in $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}$ (e.g., $k_{x}/k_{y}<0$ in figure 1). When subject to the sheared background flow $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}$ , this leading wave experiences a rotation of its wavevector until it is completely aligned (or anti-aligned) with the flow direction, when it is said to “swing” (middle panel, figure 1). When a vortical wave swings, it becomes coupled to an acoustic wave, allowing energy to be exchanged between these two branches of the dispersion relation. This appears as a spontaneous excitation of density fluctuations, because energy is being pumped into a wave that strongly perturbs the density (the acoustic wave) from one that does not (the vortical wave). Following this conversion, the shear continues to rotate the resultant acoustic wave and the flow-perpendicular component of the wavevector changes sign from its initial condition to become “trailing” (right panel, figure 1). This trailing acoustic wave is a direct, non-rotating-flow analog of the spiral density waves that we study in this work.

*Figure 1: Diagram showing the spontaneous excitation of density waves for a linearly sheared background flow $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}$ . An initially leading vortical wave, which only weakly perturbs the density, is sheared by the flow. When it swings, all or some of its wave energy is converted into an acoustic wave, which strongly perturbs the density. The choice of axes mimics that of the shearing sheet, which we introduce in §2.*

The above conversion process was first generalized to include Keplerian rotation by Bodo et al. (2005), however it was Heinemann & Papaloizou (2009a) (hereafter H&P) who demonstrated (both through analytic theory and simulation) that the excitation of spiral density waves should actually be commonplace in turbulent accretion flows. The authors found that MRI turbulence supplies the requisite fluctuations in vorticity, albeit in a slightly modified form specific to differentially rotating flows known as the pseudo-potential vorticity (or PPV). They demonstrated that fluctuations in the PPV grow slowly due to nonlinearities in MRI turbulence, and when those fluctuations swing due to the background flow shear, they are similarly converted into MHD fast waves, the magnetized-plasma equivalent of an acoustic wave. Just as in Chagelishvili et al. (1997), this manifests as the sudden appearance of a propagating density fluctuation, which in an accretion flow takes on the form of a spiral wave. Using the ideal MHD equations, H&P were able to describe the conversion process analytically, later verifying their results using MHD simulations in Heinemann & Papaloizou (2009b).

### 1.2 Non-LTE Plasma Physics of Accretion Flows

One shortcoming of prior studies of accretion-flow spiral density waves is that they assume that the plasma satisfies LTE at all times. Although the exact conditions of black-hole accretion flows are not observed directly, early analytic studies and the MHD-based simulations that followed have indicated that low-luminosity accretion flows are likely to be exceptionally hot (ion temperatures $T_{\rm i}\sim 10^{9-12}$ K) and diffuse (ion densities $n_{\rm i}\sim 10^{6-8}~\rm cm^{-3}$ ) in their equatorial plane (Rees et al., 1982; Narayan & Yi, 1994; Hawley & Balbus, 2002; Mościbrodzka et al., 2009; Pu et al., 2016; Chael et al., 2018; White et al., 2020, see, e.g.,). In such plasmas, the relatively low densities and high temperatures make the collisional mean free path ( $\lambda_{\rm mfp,i}$ ) much larger than the event horizon of the central supermassive black hole. In fact, given the above parameters, $\lambda_{\rm mfp,i}$ is at least $50\;\mu\rm pc\approx 10\;au$ , in excess of all characteristic scales of the accretion flow within ${\sim}100r_{g}$ (the gravitational radius for a $4.3\times 10^{6}~{\rm M}_{\odot}$ black hole is $r_{g}\equiv 2GM_{\bullet}/c^{2}\sim 0.1~{\rm au}$ ). Such a plasma can by no means be expected to remain in LTE, which is required for the MHD equations to be strictly valid. A non-LTE treatment of these regions may be needed to model spiral density waves in accretion flows accurately.

Spiral density waves are most likely to be affected by two non-LTE processes: resonant wave–particle interactions, and anisotropic-pressure stresses. Resonant wave–particle interactions arise because the phase-space distribution of particles (in position and velocity) is free to be rearranged by a wave. Individual particles that possess velocities slightly slower than a given wave’s phase velocity are accelerated by its ponderomotive force, while those that move slightly faster are decelerated (Vlasov, 1938). The tendency for stable distributions to be monotonic decreasing in energy ensures that more particles are moving slightly slower than the phase velocity, therefore these kinds of resonant interactions tend to extract net energy from the wave. This process is generally referred to as Landau damping (Landau, 1946), whose most common manifestation results from the force of the wave’s electric field. There are, however, alternative means by which a ponderomotive force can arise, such as through the magnetic mirror force of a compressive wave. The mirror force arises because collisionless, Larmor-gyrating particles have a conserved magnetic dipole moment, so any change in the magnetic-field strength effectively exerts a force on the particle’s gyro-center in much the same way it would if the particle were replaced by a dipole magnet. In collisionless waves this force can lead to a form of damping often referred to as “transit-time” or “Barnes” damping (Barnes, 1966). In general, any source of inertial or non-inertial field-aligned acceleration that yields a ponderomotive force can contribute to the resonant damping of a collisionless plasma wave, and the waves studied here will involve a combination of several ponderomotive forces. Importantly, however, all forms of Landau damping originate from a re-structuring of the distribution function, so none of them can be accurately captured by a fluid approach such as MHD.

On the other hand, the consequences of pressure anisotropy can be captured by a fluid model, so long as a magnetic field is present to restrict momentum transport to occur predominantly along field lines. In such cases, the thermal pressure tensor is dominated by its components parallel to ( $p_{\|}$ ) and perpendicular to ( $p_{\perp}$ ) the local magnetic-field direction (Chew et al., 1956). This aspect alone leads to a restructuring of wave eigenmodes, due to the need to accommodate an additional evolution equation (Hunana et al., 2019; Majeski et al., 2023). These pressures are therefore also free to disagree with one another – in fact, their very evolution is governed by conflicting invariants that guarantee pressure anisotropy ( $\Delta p=p_{\perp}-p_{\|}\neq 0$ ) in the presence of density ( $\rho$ ) or magnetic-field strength ( $B$ ) fluctuations. The most well-known consequence of this pressure anisotropy is the viscous stress, which has long been understood as a source of dissipation in non-LTE plasmas. Therefore, like resonant interactions, pressure anisotropy and its associated viscous stress can lead to a damping of spiral density waves.

When the ratio of thermal pressure to magnetic pressure (known as $\beta_{(\perp,\|)}\equiv 8\pi p_{(\perp,\|)}/B^{2}$ ) is $\gtrsim 1$ , $\Delta p$ takes on an additional role: a potent source of small-scale instability. Specifically, whenever $|\Delta p|$ becomes comparable to the energy density of the magnetic field, ion-Larmor-scale instabilities known as the mirror and firehose are triggered (Parker, 1958; Barnes, 1966, e.g.,). Their thresholds for instability in a high- $\beta$ plasma are given by (Southwood & Kivelson, 1993; Bott et al., 2024)

$$ \frac{\Delta p}{p_{\|}}\gtrsim\beta_{\perp}^{-1}\;{\rm(mirror)},\quad\frac{\Delta p}{p_{\|}}\lesssim-1.4\beta_{\|}^{-1}\;{\rm(firehose)}. $$

While the underlying physics of these instabilities are distinct (Rosin et al., 2011; Rincon et al., 2015), their consequences for the large-scale evolution of plasma thermodynamics are similar (Kunz et al., 2014). Both instabilities perturb the magnetic-field on sufficiently small scales that the Larmor motions of ions are disturbed. These perturbations induce pitch-angle scattering of particles with respect to the magnetic-field direction (at a rate we denote by $\nu_{\rm eff}$ ), which inevitably results in partial isotropization of the thermal pressures (Schekochihin et al., 2008; Rosin et al., 2011; Kunz et al., 2014; Riquelme et al., 2015; Rincon et al., 2015; Melville et al., 2016). In other words, a collisionless, high- $\beta$ plasma may be free of actual Coulomb collisions, but it may not be free of scattering. To avoid confusion then, in what follows we reserve the term “collisions” to describe Coulombic particle interactions exclusively, while “scattering” always refers to the isotropization of particle velocities caused by micro-instabilities. The rate at which micro-instability-induced scattering occurs is governed by the fact that it reduces the pressure anisotropy until $\Delta p$ is marginally unstable. Kunz et al. (2014) found that a balance is ultimately established between the adiabatic driving and pitch-angle isotropization of $\Delta p$ , which is achieved when the scattering rate satisfies

$$ \nu_{\rm eff}\sim\beta|3\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$:$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}|. $$

Here, $u$ is the bulk flow velocity, $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}$ is the magnetic-field unit vector, and we have used the fact that at high $\beta$ , the thresholds (1) become very stringent, so $\beta_{\perp}\approx\beta_{\|}\approx\beta$ . In the presence of magnetic-field and density fluctuations that arise due to MRI turbulence, or even spiral density waves themselves, accretion flows may feature a significant amount of pressure anisotropy and therefore instability-mediated scattering (Sharma et al., 2006; Kunz et al., 2016; Kempski et al., 2019; Dhruv et al., 2025). This scattering not only modifies the pressure anisotropy, but can also interrupt the wave–particle resonances that drive Landau/Barnes damping (Kunz et al., 2020; Majeski et al., 2023). Therefore, a careful investigation of spiral density waves in hot accretion flows must not only consider inherently large-scale effects such as resonant-wave particle interactions and viscous stresses, but also how micro-scale instabilities and their associated scattering modify those large-scale effects.

### 1.3 Overview

To reveal how non-LTE plasma physics affects the propagation, excitation, and damping of spiral density waves, we solve for the evolution of such waves in a local shearing-sheet model using semi-analytical techniques. In §2, we introduce the governing equations used to incorporate the aforementioned non-LTE physics into our models, namely kinetic MHD (Kulsrud, 1983, KMHD;) and Braginskii-MHD (Braginskii, 1965), both within the shearing-sheet approximation. Using these equations, in §3 we solve for the linear evolution of spiral density waves in non-LTE accretion flows, beginning in §3.1 with the case of a laminar/azimuthal background magnetic field. Section 3.1 is further divided into two scenarios depending on the presence or absence of scattering from micro-instabilities: in §3.1.1 we obtain spiral-wave solutions in both low- and high- $\beta$ plasmas assuming that no scattering of any kind is present, while in §3.1.2 we revisit the high- $\beta$ case including self-consistent scattering from micro-instabilities that are driven by the pressure anisotropy self-generated by the spiral waves. In §3.2 we study spiral waves in a high- $\beta$ , turbulent plasma whose “background” magnetic field is isotropically tangled and the pressure anisotropy is dominated by the contributions from the turbulent shear and Keplerian shear. We discuss the consequences of our findings in both §3 and §4. Among them are the predictions that, compared to MHD, the excitation of non-LTE spiral waves in high- $\beta$ , turbulent accretion flows is significantly suppressed by viscous dissipation (perhaps then contributing less to emission variability), and that the pattern speed of synchrotron structures in the emission region should be smaller than that predicted by MHD. Importantly, Landau/Barnes damping is not found to be an efficient mechanism by which these spiral density waves can be dissipated in collisionless accretion flows. Instead, the dominant form of damping is viscous, a result of particle scattering induced by the mirror and firehose instabilities that are naturally driven by collisionless MRI turbulence. A consequence is that, in low- $\beta$ accretion flows where micro-instabilities are more difficult to excite and so the dominant form of density-wave damping is more likely to be Landau/Barnes damping, spiral density waves are not suppressed. In §5, we summarize our investigation and consider next steps that should be taken.

## 2 Model Equations in the Shearing Sheet

Due to the added complexity of capturing relativistic effects near the central object, this work does not attempt a global model of spiral density waves in black-hole accretion flows. Instead, similarly to H&P, we employ the non-relativistic shearing-sheet approximation to study the local excitation and damping of spiral waves prior to their propagation into the emission region (Goldreich & Lynden-Bell, 1965). In the shearing sheet, the dynamical equations are transformed into a frame that rotates with the flow at a cylindrical-radial distance $r_{0}$ from the central object, which is much larger than the spatial extent of the domain being studied. This allows coordinate curvature to be neglected while incorporating the Coriolis force and a linear approximation to the difference between the centrifugal and gravitational forces. Rotation is taken to be about the $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}$ axis at a steady rate $\Omega(r)$ . The radial variation in $\Omega$ away from its value $\Omega_{0}$ at $r_{0}$ is approximated by a linear shear in the azimuthal flow, and, either by assumption or via spatial averaging, we do not consider variation in the $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}$ direction—hence the name “shearing sheet.” The simplicity afforded by this local approach allows us to focus on the complexity added by the effects discussed in §1.2, namely, anisotropic pressures, resonant wave–particle damping, and Larmor-scale instabilities. We now describe the two models that we use to capture the aforementioned effects: one appropriate to situations in which $\nu_{\rm eff}$ is not large enough to preclude resonant interactions (kinetic MHD), and one appropriate to situations when it is (Braginskii-MHD).

### 2.1 Kinetic MHD

If the effective scattering frequency $\nu_{\rm eff}$ is smaller than or comparable to the characteristic dynamical frequency (viz., $\nu_{\rm eff}\lesssim v_{\rm th,i}/l$ , with $l$ the characteristic dynamical length, $v_{\rm th,i}=\sqrt{2T_{\rm i}/m_{\rm i}}$ the ion thermal speed, and $m_{\rm i}$ the ion mass), model equations must be used that account for collisionless effects such as resonant damping and non-LTE structure in velocity space. Kinetic magnetohydrodynamics (Kulsrud, 1983, KMHD;) provides such a set of equations, and applies when the dynamical timescales ( $\omega^{-1}$ ) and lengthscales ( $\ell$ ) are extremely large compared to those associated with the Larmor motions of individual charged particles, viz. $\omega\ll\omega_{\rm L}$ and $l\gg r_{\rm L}$ , where $\omega_{\rm L}$ and $r_{\rm L}$ are the Larmor frequency and radius. This well-magnetized limit is particularly suited for low-luminosity accretion flows. Consider Sgr A∗ as an example (EHT et al., 2024): the orbital frequency $\Omega$ (which approximates $\omega$ ) is ${\sim}10^{-3}\rm\;rad/s$ at $10\,r_{g}$ , while the Larmor frequency of ions at $10\,r_{g}$ is ${\sim}10^{6}\;\rm rad/s$ (Sen et al., 2025, assuming $B\approx 25\rm\;G$ ; ). This scale separation is satisfied even more handily for the electrons, however we do not model electrons through a kinetic approach in this work. In low-luminosity accretion flows, the electron temperature is thought to be much smaller than that of the ions (Quataert & Gruzinov, 1999; Howes, 2010; Kawazura et al., 2020), so the electron pressure is negligible and their primary role is simply to screen the field-aligned component of the electric field (which in turn removes the “classical” channel of Landau damping, but does not affect others, such as transit-time damping). It is therefore unnecessary to solve for the electron distribution function here, so all references to a distribution function concern that of the ions alone.

In addition to the aforementioned length- and time-scale separation, another central feature of KMHD is that bulk plasma motions ( $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}})$ ) are separated from individual particle velocities ( $v$ ) so that the resultant distribution function is solved for in the (non-inertial) frame of $u$ . This is accomplished by exchanging $v$ in favor of the peculiar velocities $\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}\equiv\mbox{\boldmath{$v$}}-\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}$ in the distribution function $f(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}},\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}})$ . Importantly, $u$ includes not only turbulence and waves, but also the background shear flow inherent to the shearing sheet approximation. Following this transformation, $f$ is then averaged over Larmor orbit gyro-phases to reduce the velocity-space dependence from $(w_{x},w_{y},w_{z})$ to $(w_{\perp},w_{\|})$ , where $\parallel$ and $\perp$ denote the directions along and across the local magnetic field. The evolution of the resultant gyrotropic distribution $f(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}},w_{\perp},w_{\|})$ is given by the drift-kinetic equation

$$ \frac{{\rm D}f}{{\rm D}t}+\frac{{\rm D}\ln B}{{\rm D}t}\frac{w_{\perp}}{2}\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_{\perp}}-\biggl[\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\biggl(\frac{{\rm D}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}}{{\rm D}t}+2\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}+4A_{0}\Omega_{0}x\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$x$}}}\biggr)+\frac{w_{\perp}^{2}}{2}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\ln B\biggr]\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_{\|}}=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)_{\!\rm scatt,eff}, $$

where ${\rm D}/{\rm D}t\equiv\partial/\partial t+\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}+w_{\|}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}$ . Here, $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$x$}}}$ represents the local radial direction, $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ the local azimuthal direction, $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}$ the vertical direction, and $A_{0}$ (Oort’s first constant) the rate of shear in the differential rotation local to $r_{0}$ ; $A_{0}=-(3/4)\Omega_{0}$ for a Keplerian flow, which we adopt uniformly throughout this work. The second term on the left-hand side of (3) accounts for the change in the perpendicular velocity of the particles in the presence of a time-dependent magnetic-field strength due to conservation of particle magnetic moments. The third term (the one in square brackets) describes field-parallel forces on the particle guiding centers, including those that arise from boosting to the non-inertial reference frame of the bulk flow (a derivation of those terms is provided in §A). Because $u$ contains the background shear flow, which is given by $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}=2A_{0}x\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ in the shearing sheet, the terms $2\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}$ and $4A_{0}\Omega_{0}x\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$x$}}}$ cancel in equilibrium, so the only direct contributions of the shearing sheet to the drift-kinetic equation are via the perturbed Coriolis force and the presence of $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}$ in the convective derivative. We have also dropped the force due to the parallel electric field, which, as mentioned earlier, is a consequence of the electron temperature being negligible compared to that of the ions. The unspecified term on the right-hand side represents the effects of particle scattering caused by micro-instabilities on the evolution of $f$ .

The evolution of the bulk flow in KMHD is given by the MHD momentum equation with a pressure tensor that is anisotropic with respect to the local magnetic-field direction:

$$ \rho\frac{{\rm d}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}}{{\rm d}t}=-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\left(p_{\perp}+\frac{B^{2}}{8\pi}\right)+\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\left[\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\biggl(p_{\perp}-p_{\parallel}+\frac{B^{2}}{4\pi}\biggr)\right]-2\rho\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}-4\rho A_{0}\Omega_{0}x\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$x$}}}, $$

where ${\rm d}/{\rm d}t\equiv\partial/\partial t+\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}$ is the convective derivative. Given our assumption of cold electrons, the $p_{(\perp,\|)}$ refer only to the anisotropic components of the ion pressure tensor. The magnetic-field induction equation is unmodified from ideal MHD:

$$ \frac{{\rm d}\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}}{{\rm d}t}=\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}-\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}. $$

To close the KMHD system, the moments of the distribution $f$ are calculated using the peculiar velocities $(w_{\perp},w_{\|})$ :

$$ \rho=m_{\rm i}\int{\rm d}^{3}w\,f\,,\quad p_{\perp}=\frac{m_{\rm i}}{2}\int{\rm d}^{3}w\,w_{\perp}^{2}f\,,\quad p_{\|}=m_{\rm i}\int{\rm d}^{3}w\,w_{\|}^{2}f\,, $$

where ${\rm d}^{3}w=2\pi w_{\perp}{\rm d}w_{\perp}{\rm d}w_{\|}$ . Because $f$ is specified in the frame of the local bulk-flow velocity, it has no velocity moments.

The scattering term that we employ in this work for the right-hand side of (3) is a version of the Krook operator that drives the perturbed distribution function toward a local Maxwellian having the same isotropic temperature and density as $f$ (Gross & Krook, 1956):

$$ \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)_{\!\rm scatt,eff}=-\nu_{\rm eff}\left[f(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}},w_{\perp},w_{\|})-F_{\rm M}(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}},w)\right],\quad{\rm where}\quad F_{\rm M}(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}},w)\equiv\frac{\rho(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}})\sqrt{m_{\rm i}}}{(2\pi T_{\rm i}(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}}))^{3/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{m_{\rm i}w^{2}}{2T_{\rm i}(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}})}\right), $$

$w^{2}\equiv w^{2}_{\perp}+w^{2}_{\|}$ , and the temperature $T_{\rm i}=(m_{\rm i}/\rho)\,p=(m_{\rm i}/\rho)(2p_{\perp}+p_{\|})/3$ . In the collisionless accretion flows studied here, the effective scattering rate, $\nu_{\rm eff}$ , refers exclusively to scattering induced by micro-instabilities. One caveat of using (7) to mimic pitch-angle scattering from micro-instabilities, however, is that pitch-angle scattering only isotropizes the distribution with respect to the magnetic field; it does not necessarily drive $f$ toward a Maxwellian. Nonetheless, when linearized, (7) affects all fluid moments of $f$ below the heat flux in a manner that exactly mimics pure pitch-angle scattering, so the consequences of this distinction are likely to be minimal in the context of the spiral waves studied here.11 1 Alternatively, a more accurate choice, at least for the firehose instability, would be the effective firehose collision operator of Bott et al. (2025) (see their equation 6.1). Their operator is much more complex, however, and, compared to our simple Krook prescription, only changes the viscous stress by an order-unity amount.

### 2.2 The Braginskii-MHD Closure

Under certain circumstances, such as $\beta\gg 1$ , the rate of scattering in (2) may be so large that the condition $l\gg v_{\rm th,i}/\nu_{\rm eff}$ is satisfied. In this case, Landau/Barnes damping may be ignored because resonant interactions are interrupted before they can damp the wave (Zakharov & Karpman, 1963), and the strong scattering keeps the pressure anisotropy much smaller than the isotropic pressure ( $p$ ). If, additionally, the flow satisfies $1\gtrsim u/v_{\rm th,i}\gg v_{\rm th,i}/(l\,\nu_{\rm eff})$ , then $\Delta p$ can be approximated by the model of Braginskii (1965):

$$ \Delta p\approx\frac{3p}{\nu_{\rm eff}}\left(\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}-\frac{1}{3}\bm{\mathsf{I}}\right)\,\mbox{\boldmath{$:$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}, $$

where $\bm{\mathsf{I}}$ is the unit dyadic. The corresponding isotropic component of the pressure is evolved according to

$$ \frac{{\rm d}p}{{\rm d}t}=\frac{5}{3}\frac{p}{\rho}\frac{{\rm d}\rho}{{\rm d}t}+\frac{2\nu_{\rm eff}}{9}\frac{(\Delta p)^{2}}{p}+\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\left[\frac{2\sigma}{3}\frac{p}{\nu_{\rm eff}}\,\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\left(\frac{p}{\rho}\right)\right], $$

where the factor $\sigma$ depends on the form of the collision operator present in the kinetic equation. For the Krook operator that we employ (7), $\sigma=5/2$ ; a more standard value is $\sigma=3.91$ , which corresponds to the linearized form of the Landau collision operator (Spitzer, 1962; Braginskii, 1965). From (9), we see that the combination of pressure anisotropy and scattering leads to irreversible heating, and that conductive heat transport occurs only along the magnetic field. By eliminating the time derivative of the pressure anisotropy in favor of a steady-state balance between its adiabatic production and its relaxation due to scattering, the Braginskii approximation represents a considerable simplification from KMHD. The closure (8) will prove useful in describing spiral density waves in the presence of a highly turbulent magnetic-field configuration, for which KMHD becomes intractable.

## 3 Linear Collisionless Shearing Waves

In this section, we solve for the propagation, damping, and—in the limit of strong scattering—turbulent excitation of spiral density waves in collisionless, differentially rotating plasmas. In all setups that we present, the waves studied possess no $z$ wavenumber. This is motivated by the fact that line-of-sight emission from waves with $k_{z}=0$ is stronger than those with a significant $k_{z}$ ; for example, Kunz et al. (2016) found in their shearing-box study of the collisionless MRI that non-axisymmetric density waves only appear after integrating over the $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}$ direction (and then only weakly still). Additionally, when considering waves in a turbulent background magnetic field (§3.2), we spatially average over the $z$ coordinate, so $k_{z}\neq 0$ waves are eliminated outright. Beyond neglecting $k_{z}$ , we adopt the standard non-modal approach that describes non-axisymmetric, linear perturbations to the background state as an initial value problem for “shearing waves” (Goldreich & Lynden-Bell, 1965; Johnson, 2007). In this approach, fluctuations in a plasma quantity $\chi$ are assumed to take the form

$$ \chi(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}})=\chi_{0}+\delta\chi(t)\,{\rm e}^{{\rm i}k_{x}(t)x+{\rm i}k_{y}y}, $$

where the radial wavenumber $k_{x}(t)=k_{x,0}-2A_{0}k_{y}t$ is time-dependent on account of the background flow shear. The primary advantage of this approach is that the spatial dependence of the parallel acceleration in (3) and (4) that is caused by the flow shear is exchanged in favor of a time dependence, reducing the governing equations to a system of time-dependent linear ODEs.

Given this approach, we consider four distinct scenarios. First, in §3.1 the background magnetic field is considered to be azimuthal and constant; this situation is amenable to an analysis using the KMHD set of equations, both when $\nu_{\rm eff}=0$ (scenario 1, §3.1.1) and when $\nu_{\rm eff}\neq 0$ (scenario 2, §3.1.2). In §3.1, we investigate the impact of damping mechanisms on only the propagation of shearing waves as they transition from leading ( $k_{x}(t)/k_{y}<0$ ) to trailing ( $k_{x}(t)/k_{y}>0$ ); the actual excitation of spiral waves is not studied. The excitation process H&P described requires a turbulent background state to supply (pseudo-potential) vorticity, which can eventually be converted into spiral waves. Being absent of turbulence and therefore vorticity, the laminar, $\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}_{0}=B_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ background state of §3.1 does not excite spiral density waves on its own. Therefore, in §3.2 we consider a turbulent background so that the spiral-wave excitation process can be studied as well. Because the KMHD equations become prohibitively difficult with which to work in the presence of a turbulent magnetic field, we only treat the limit of strong micro-instability scattering in §3.2 so that the simplifying approximation of Braginskii-MHD may be employed. With Braginskii-MHD, we first investigate the evolution of initially leading density waves similarly to scenarios 1 and 2 (scenario 3, §3.2.1), allowing us to study the effects of damping alone. Once damping in the turbulent background field is well understood, we study initially leading vorticity fluctuations (scenario 4, §3.2.3), which are converted into spiral density waves and therefore serve as a combined study of damping and excitation. Altogether then, this work presents a study of the damping of collisionless spiral density waves in two extremes: laminar magnetic fields and isotropically tangled magnetic fields.

For ease of notation, we henceforth drop all “0” subscripts on the local rotation and shear frequencies, $\Omega_{0}\rightarrow\Omega$ and $A_{0}\rightarrow A$ .

### 3.1 Azimuthal Background Magnetic Field

Beginning with the laminar azimuthal background magnetic field $\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}_{0}=B_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ , we linearize the KMHD system (3)–(6) about the equilibrium shear flow $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}=2Ax\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ and an isotropic Maxwellian background distribution, $f(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}},w_{\perp},w_{\|})=F_{\rm M,0}(w)+\delta f(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}},w_{\perp},w_{\|})$ , and insert the assumption of shearing waveforms (10).22 2 It is likely that the actual distribution function $f$ in a collisionless accretion flow is not a small perturbation away from a Maxwellian. However, the regulation of temperature anisotropy by small-scale instabilities limits the ratio $T_{\perp}/T_{\|}$ to be very nearly unity on average (Kunz et al., 2016). For these reasons, we make the simplifying assumption that the background distribution is an isotropic Maxwellian. In the absence of scattering, the resultant system of equations is:

$$ \biggl(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+{\rm i}k_{y}w_{\|}\biggr)\delta f+\Biggl[2{\rm i}\biggl(\frac{w_{\|}}{v_{\rm th,i}}\biggr)^{2}k_{y}\delta u_{y}+{\rm i}\biggl(\frac{w_{\perp}}{v_{\rm th,i}}\biggr)^{2}(k_{x}-2Ak_{y}t)\delta u_{x}-{\rm i}k_{y}w_{\|}\frac{\delta p_{\|}}{p_{0}}+2A\frac{\delta B_{x}}{B_{0}}\biggl(\frac{2w_{\|}^{2}-w_{\perp}^{2}}{v_{\rm th,i}^{2}}\biggr)\Biggr]F_{\rm M,0}=0, \frac{{\rm d}\delta u_{x}}{{\rm d}t}=-{\rm i}(k_{x}-2Ak_{y}t)\biggl(\frac{\delta p_{\perp}}{\rho_{0}}+\frac{B_{0}\delta B_{y}}{4\pi\rho_{0}}\biggr)+{\rm i}k_{y}\frac{B_{0}\delta B_{x}}{4\pi\rho_{0}}+2\Omega\delta u_{y}, \frac{{\rm d}\delta u_{y}}{{\rm d}t}=-{\rm i}k_{y}\frac{\delta p_{\|}}{\rho_{0}}-2(\Omega+A)\delta u_{x}, \frac{{\rm d}\delta B_{x}}{{\rm d}t}={\rm i}k_{y}B_{0}\delta u_{x}, k_{y}\delta B_{y}=-(k_{x}-2Ak_{y}t)\delta B_{x}. $$

In (11e), we have used the solenoidality condition on the perturbed magnetic field, rather than the induction equation, to obtain the $y$ component of the magnetic field.

In all solutions obtained while employing this azimuthal $\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}_{0}$ configuration, we use the same initial conditions for the spiral wave: a leading perturbation is initialized to $u_{x}$ alone, with $k_{x,0}=-10k_{y}$ . This excites a fast magnetosonic wave (the MHD/KMHD analog of an acoustic wave), which we evolve until the radial wavenumber is exactly reversed ( $k_{x}=10k_{y}$ ).33 3 In the collisionless limit, the $k_{z}=0$ shearing fast wave is entirely decoupled from the non-axisymmetric MRI (Balbus & Hawley, 1992), so we need not worry about instability affecting our investigation of collisionless damping. In ideal MHD, however, Mamatsashvili et al. (2026) have shown the two waves to be coupled, and swing-amplified MRI fluctuations at least partially convert into spiral density waves for laminar magnetic-field configurations. Although we vary other parameters, like the ratios $\Omega/k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}$ and $\beta$ , we do not modify the initial wavenumber ratio.

When scattering effects are included, the density and temperature in (7) are perturbed to obtain the linearized Krook operator:

$$ \left(\frac{\partial\delta f}{\partial t}\right)_{\rm scatt,eff}\approx-\nu_{\rm eff}\left[\delta f(t,w_{\perp},w_{\|})-F_{\rm M,0}(w)\left(\frac{\delta\rho}{\rho_{0}}-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\delta T}{T_{0}}+\frac{w^{2}}{v_{\rm th,i}^{2}}\frac{\delta T}{T_{0}}\right)\right], $$

which is appended to the right-hand side of (11a) when necessary. Although the above system is significantly simplified from (3), it is still not analytically tractable in general. Therefore, we pursue numerical solutions to (11) as initial value problems using a Hermite–Laguerre polynomial decomposition technique (see Appendix A of Majeski et al. 2023 for a description of this method as applied to the non-shearing-sheet KMHD equations).

#### 3.1.1 Solutions for $\nu_{\rm eff}=0$

We first present solutions to the system (11) without any scattering ( $\nu_{\rm eff}=0$ ).

*Figure 2: Evolution of KMHD (solid) and ideal MHD (dashed) spiral density waves in an azimuthal magnetic field with $\beta=5$ , initialized as leading $\delta u_{x}=0.1v_{\rm th,i}$ perturbations. The vertical dotted line denotes the swing time when $k_{x}(t)=0$ . Moderate damping due to resonant wave–particle interaction is reflected in the fact that at late times the KMHD wave amplitude is noticeably lower than that of the MHD wave.*

To orient the reader, in figure 2 we present the (numerically solved) evolution of an example collisionless leading fast wave (solid lines) with $k_{y}=\Omega/v_{\rm th,i}$ in a plasma with $\beta=5$ (here, $\beta=\beta_{\perp,0}=\beta_{\|,0}$ is that of the uniform background state). The density fluctuation (top panel) behaves in a manner that is largely typical of shearing density waves: being excited at $|k_{x}|\gg k_{y}$ , its frequency $\omega$ , which is proportional to $|k|$ , decreases over time as $|k_{x}|$ decreases from the shear. As it does so its amplitude decreases, a consequence of (near) conservation of wave action preserving the ratio $E/\omega$ (Johnson, 2007; Heinemann & Papaloizou, 2009a, with $E$ the energy of the wave perturbation;). The amplitude reaches a minimum at the swing time when $k_{x}=0$ , which is marked by the vertical dotted line, and then begins to grow again from wave-action conservation. The behavior of $\delta u_{x}$ and $\delta u_{y}$ is also predictable: at early times when $|k_{x}|\gg k_{y}$ , the flow perturbation is dominated by its radial component $\delta u_{x}$ , although it exchanges energy with the azimuthal perturbation $\delta u_{y}$ when $|k_{x}|\ll k_{y}$ . We also solve the exact same initial value problem for an MHD plasma (dashed lines). Much of the behavior is similar, however the wave frequencies are slightly different and, more importantly, the MHD wave has a noticeably larger amplitude than the KMHD wave at the end of its evolution. This difference results from the collisionless damping in KMHD that is absent from ideal MHD, which, when present, also breaks perfect wave action conservation in the collisionless wave. Seeing as the collisionless wave amplitude appears to grow from action conservation at a similar rate to the MHD wave long after the swing, it seems that most of the damping must have occurred when $|k_{x}|\lesssim k_{y}$ .

The example shown in figure 2, although illustrative, does not reveal fully the underlying physics of how collisionless damping operates in these waves. Furthermore, it is valuable to generalize these results to a range of $\beta$ and $\Omega/k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}$ . This generalization can be accomplished both by an (approximate) analytic description, and by a survey of numerical solutions with a similar setup but varied parameters. In what follows, we take both approaches to explore the problem more thoroughly, beginning with the former.

The analytic approach we adopt is a lowest-order WKB approximation, where we solve for the damping of these collisionless fast waves in the limit of slow shear compared to the field-parallel sound-crossing time, i.e., $|A|\ll k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}$ . The WKB approximation is frequently used to describe sheared waves in accretion flows, especially the non-axisymmetric MRI (Balbus & Hawley, 1992; Kim & Ostriker, 2000; Johnson & Gammie, 2005; Balbus & Hawley, 2006, e.g.,). For the MRI, however, the common choice for a WKB parameter is $k_{y}/|k_{x}|\ll 1$ . Because the damping of spiral waves appears strongest when $|k_{x}|\lesssim k_{y}$ , we must instead use the low-shear approximation (similarly to H&P). As is typical of lowest-order WKB approximations, our steps are to first solve for the instantaneous (complex) frequency of these waves given a constant $k_{x}$ , then restore the time dependence of $k_{x}(t)$ and integrate the wave eikonal forward in time to obtain the evolution of the wave. Because we are concerned with damping, our focus will be on the complex part of the frequency. Without further ado, we now neglect $A$ to leading order in the linearized system (11), and substitute perturbations of the form $\delta\chi(t)=\delta\chi\exp(-{\rm i}\omega t)$ . After taking the appropriate moments of $\delta f$ , the resultant system can be solved for the instantaneous dispersion relation:

$$ \biggl\{\zeta^{2}-\frac{1}{\beta}\biggl(1+\frac{k_{x}^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}}\biggr)+\frac{k_{x}^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}}\,\zeta Z(\zeta)+8\zeta^{2}\biggl(\frac{\Omega}{k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}}\biggr)^{2}\bigl[1+\zeta Z(\zeta)\bigr]\biggr\}\biggl(\zeta^{2}-\frac{1}{\beta}\biggr)\equiv\epsilon(\zeta,\mbox{\boldmath{$k$}})=0. $$

Here, $\zeta\equiv\omega/(k_{y}v_{\rm th,i})$ and $Z(\zeta)\equiv\pi^{-1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}{\rm d}x\,\exp(-x^{2})/(x-\zeta)$ is the “plasma dispersion function.” The Alfvén-wave solution, given by $\zeta=\pm\beta^{-1/2}$ in the right-most parentheses of (13), decouples from the compressive fluctuations (in curly brackets) given our assumptions. With $\Omega\sim|A|$ in a Keplerian flow, one could also drop the $\Omega$ term in (13); for the sake of generality, however, we retain it for now. Because of the non-analytic nature of the plasma dispersion function, we can only obtain approximations to the instantaneous frequency of these fast waves. Given that only a small amount of damping occurs in figure 2 over many periods of the wave, let us then adopt the simplifying assumption $\zeta_{r}\gg\zeta_{i}$ (with the subscripts “ $r$ ” and “ $i$ ” denoting real and imaginary parts). Expanding the dispersion relation about $\zeta\approx\zeta_{r}$ leads to

$$ \epsilon(\zeta,\mbox{\boldmath{$k$}})\approx\epsilon(\zeta_{r},\mbox{\boldmath{$k$}})+{\rm i}\zeta_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial\zeta}\epsilon(\zeta_{r},\mbox{\boldmath{$k$}})\approx 0. $$

The assumption that $\zeta_{i}\ll\zeta_{r}$ is consistent with taking $\epsilon_{i}\ll\epsilon_{r}$ , so that the real and imaginary parts of this equation become

$$ \epsilon_{r}(\zeta_{r},\mbox{\boldmath{$k$}})\approx 0\,\qquad\mathrm{and}\qquad\zeta_{i}\approx-\frac{\epsilon_{i}(\zeta_{r},\mbox{\boldmath{$k$}})}{\partial_{\zeta_{r}}\epsilon_{r}(\zeta_{r},\mbox{\boldmath{$k$}})}. $$

$Z(\zeta)$ is still non-analytic, so we expand in the limit of $|\zeta_{r}|\gg 1$ (the validity conditions for which we determine a posteriori) and solve for the wave frequency to obtain

$$ \zeta_{r}\approx\pm\sqrt{\frac{1}{\beta}\left(1+\frac{k_{x}^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}}\right)+\frac{k_{x}^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}}+\frac{4\Omega^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}v_{\rm th,i}^{2}}}. $$

To determine when (16) is valid, the minimum value of $|\zeta_{r}|$ occurs when $k_{x}=0$ , giving $|\zeta_{r}|\geq\sqrt{\beta^{-1}+4\Omega^{2}/k_{y}^{2}v_{\rm th,i}^{2}}$ . Given that we have already assumed $|A|\sim\Omega\ll k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}$ , the expansion of $Z(\zeta)$ that we have employed is acceptable when $\beta\lesssim 1$ . We now insert equation (16) into the second equation of (15) to obtain

$$ \zeta_{i}=-\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\biggl\{\frac{|k_{x}|}{k_{y}}+\frac{8\Omega^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}v_{\rm th,i}^{2}}\biggl[\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{|k_{x}|}{k_{y}}\biggl(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\biggr)+\frac{4\Omega^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}v_{\rm th,i}^{2}}\biggr]\biggr\}\exp\biggl[-\frac{1}{\beta}-\frac{k_{x}^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}}\biggl(1+\frac{1}{\beta}\biggr)-\frac{4\Omega^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}v_{\rm th,i}^{2}}\biggr]. $$

Because all terms in the exponential are negative, $\zeta_{i}$ is largest when those terms are most nearly zero. Given a $\beta$ and $\Omega/k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}$ , the strongest damping therefore occurs when $|k_{x}|/k_{y}\ll 1$ , and the wavevector is most nearly aligned with the azimuthal background field. Physically, this is because the ponderomotive force that drives Landau/Barnes damping also becomes aligned with the field direction when $k_{x}=0$ , and so the resonant ions, which can only move freely along $B$ , are able to respond to that force maximally. As $|k_{x}|$ grows however, the force misaligns with $B$ , and the exponential term rapidly becomes small, hence why there are no obvious signs of damping at early or late times in figure 2. Additionally, although (17) is only valid at moderate to low $\beta$ , we can again see from the exponential that moderate $\beta$ leads to more damping than very low $\beta$ (due to the $-\beta^{-1}$ term). This can be attributed to the fact that thermal fluctuations contribute more to the wave energy at $\beta\sim 1$ than they do at $\beta\ll 1$ , so any damping of those thermal fluctuations by resonances in the distribution function will have a more significant impact on the wave at larger $\beta$ . In fact, although (17) is not valid in the limit $\beta\gg 1$ , the previous statement still implies that once the magnetic field contributes a negligible amount to the wave energy, $\zeta_{i}$ should become effectively independent of $\beta$ because only the thermal contributions will matter. In that limit, the damping rate must instead be found by dropping the term $\propto\beta^{-1}$ in the curly braces of (13), and numerically solving for $\zeta$ , which will be a function of only $\Omega/k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}$ and $k_{x}/k_{y}$ (or, considering the Keplerian WKB limit, $k_{x}/k_{y}$ alone).

With an expression for $\zeta_{i}(k_{x})$ in hand, the final step in estimating the role of damping in our current spiral wave setup is to integrate the eikonal $-\zeta_{i}(k_{x}(t))k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}{\rm d}t$ forward in time as is typical of the WKB approximation. Using the shearing wavenumber relationship $k_{x}(t)=k_{x,0}-2Ak_{y}t$ , this time integral can be exchanged in favor of an integral over $k_{x}$ , which we provide here for a symmetric interval about $k_{x}=0$ :

$$ \delta\rho(t{=}k_{x,0}/Ak_{y})=\delta\rho(t{=}0)\exp\left[\frac{1}{2Ak_{y}}\int\limits_{k_{x,0}}^{-k_{x,0}}{\rm d}k_{x}\,\zeta_{i}(k_{x})k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}\right]. $$

We have given (18) for a symmetric interval about $k_{x}=0$ because it would not be strictly correct otherwise: as we alluded to in the discussion of figure 2, wave-action conservation causes the amplitude of a spiral density wave to change in time in a manner that is symmetric about the swing time. Because wave-action conservation does not lead to damping, it does not contribute to the suppression of spiral density waves. We therefore remove its effect by considering how the amplitude of our spiral density wave changes between $k_{x}(t)=k_{x,0}$ and $-k_{x,0}$ .44 4 For a detailed discussion of the role of wave-action conservation in sheared MHD waves, see Johnson (2007). We lastly note that, because (17) has a Gaussian form in $k_{x}$ , the integral (18) can technically be evaluated analytically. For finite $k_{x,0}/k_{y}$ however, its form is much too cumbersome to include explicitly, so we leave the reader to evaluate it analytically or numerically as they deem necessary. Regardless, the dependence of the cumulative damping on $\beta$ and $k_{x}/k_{y}$ remains similar to that found in the discussion of (17).

*Figure 3: Efficiency of transfer from leading to trailing for fast waves with $\nu_{\rm eff}=0$ , as a function of $\beta$ and $k_{y}$ . Damping is most effective for large- $k_{y}$ waves because they experience a larger number of wave periods for a given time over which $k_{x}(t)\rightarrow-k_{x,0}$ . The dashed and dash-dotted lines are WKB predictions of the $\rm T=0.1$ curves in the low-to-moderate $\beta$ and high- $\beta$ limits, respectively. The lack of damping at low $k_{y}$ indicates that Landau/Barnes damping may not significantly affect spiral waves excited by the process described in H&P.*

Having discussed the damping of the collisionless fast wave analytically, we now perform a survey of numerical solutions to this problem over $\beta$ and $\Omega$ to see these effects in practice. In figure 3, we integrate the full set of equations (11) numerically to calculate the amount of damping that is incurred by fast waves over a range of $\beta$ and $k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}/\Omega$ for a period of time that is symmetric about the swing time ( $k_{x}=-10k_{y}\rightarrow 10k_{y}$ ). Dissipation is measured in terms of the following quantity:

$$ {\rm T}\equiv\frac{|\delta\rho_{\textrm{p-p}}(t{=}k_{x,0}/Ak_{y})|}{|\delta\rho_{\textrm{p-p}}(t{=}0)|}, $$

which measures the fraction of the density wave amplitude that is successfully transferred from leading to trailing. Here, the subscript “p-p” refers to the fact that we use the peak-to-peak amplitudes of the waves at the beginning and end of the numerical solution to determine $\rm T$ .55 5 This measure for $\rm T$ motivates the choice $k_{x}=-10k_{y}\rightarrow 10k_{y}$ for the evolution of our fast mode. A shorter evolution interval means relatively few wave periods before and after the swing from which to calculate the peak-to-peak amplitude. As mentioned earlier, with the wave evolved for a period centered on the swing time, the effects of action conservation on the amplitude are irrelevant. The most clear trend in figure 3 is that large- $k_{y}$ (or alternatively small- $\Omega$ ) waves are the ones that are most effectively damped. This comes about because the number of wave periods they experience during a swing (when damping is strongest) is larger than for a wave with small $k_{y}$ , so, given the same ratio $|\zeta_{i}|/\zeta_{r}$ , more of the fast-wave energy can be lost during the swing to Landau/Barnes damping. By comparison, this also means that lower- $k_{y}$ waves, which swing quickly compared to their oscillation, are more weakly damped. As anticipated from Equation (17), as well as our discussion of the alternative $\beta\gg 1$ limit, damping also becomes more effective as $\beta$ increases from $\ll 1$ to $\sim 1$ , eventually steadying once $\beta\gg 1$ . To compare to our WKB approximation, we include a dashed line representing the prediction for $\rm T=0.1$ that is obtained by evaluating the integral (18) given the damping rate (17). At low, and surprisingly even moderate $\beta$ , this estimate yields a reasonable approximation to the actual $\rm T=0.1$ curve from the numerical simulations. We also evaluate the same integral (18) for a numerical solution to (13) that neglects the $\beta^{-1}$ term (a high- $\beta$ approximation). The prediction that it yields for $\rm T=0.1$ (the dash-dotted line) is a good approximation to the numerical solutions of (11) in the high- $\beta$ limit.

Perhaps the most important finding that we have obtained in this section is that Landau/Barnes damping is inefficient at damping spiral waves with moderate-to-low values of $k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}/\Omega$ , a consequence of their relatively brief time spent with $\mbox{\boldmath{$k$}}\,\|\,\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}_{0}$ . This is especially notable given that H&P found the spiral-wave excitation process in MHD to be most effective for waves having $k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}/\Omega\sim 1$ . Accordingly, in an accretion flow that is free of particle scattering and that possesses a relatively uniform, dominantly azimuthal field, Landau/Barnes damping is not expected to damp spiral waves significantly. We now test whether this conclusion still holds in the presence of particle scattering.

#### 3.1.2 Solutions for Wave-driven $\nu_{\rm eff}$

In the presence of sufficient scattering ( $\nu_{\rm eff}\gtrsim|\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$k$}}|\,v_{\rm th,i}$ ), the resonances that drive Landau/Barnes damping are interrupted and the dominant damping mechanism becomes viscous damping. As a fast wave propagates, it generates pressure anisotropy through the approximate conservation of the particle adiabatic invariants (Chew et al., 1956). Scattering, on the other hand, isotropizes the distribution, and therefore the pressure tensor, effectively thermalizing the portion of the wave energy responsible for producing that pressure anisotropy and viscously damping the wave. Unlike Landau/Barnes damping, viscous damping can occur regardless of the wavevector’s alignment with the magnetic field. It is therefore not limited to operating near the swing time, but rather can occur even when the wave is leading or trailing. Considering this extended range of wavenumbers over which viscous damping occurs then, a spiral density wave that is subject to weak scattering may experience more damping than one that is entirely free of scattering (or alternatively, one in which scattering is so strong that LTE is enforced at all times, e.g., the MHD solution of figure 2).

As discussed in §1.2, the accretion-flow environments that we investigate here are practically free of Coulomb collisions. Therefore, any scattering that may be present is instead expected to be a result of pressure-anisotropy-triggered micro-instabilities (e.g., the mirror and firehose). The unperturbed background state that we study in this section, namely $\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}_{0}=B_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ and $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}=2Ax\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ , does not produce any pressure anisotropy on its own because $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}_{0}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$:$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}=0$ . However, fast magnetosonic waves do produce a fluctuating pressure anisotropy as they propagate, and at sufficiently high $\beta$ , that pressure anisotropy can become large enough in magnitude to surpass the mirror and firehose instability thresholds (1). In Majeski et al. (2023), the authors found that a fast wave propagating perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field produces enough $\Delta p$ to trigger the mirror and firehose instabilities when it perturbs the magnetic field such that $|\delta B|/B_{0}\gtrsim 2/\beta$ . Similarly, high- $\beta$ fast waves propagating parallel to the magnetic field (also known as ion-acoustic waves) trigger micro-instabilities whenever $|\delta\rho|/\rho_{0}\gtrsim 2/\beta$ (Kunz et al., 2020). At $\beta\gtrsim 10$ , fast waves with supercritical amplitudes can still be reasonably treated according to linear theory, because the timescales associated with nonlinear processes, such as wave steepening, remain larger than the linear wave period. As we saw in figure 2, shearing-wave amplitudes are not constant in time, so a generic amplitude limit cannot be as easily defined here. Nonetheless, we can still investigate how self-generated micro-instabilities and their scattering affect the propagation and damping of spiral density waves of various amplitudes in the azimuthal- $\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}_{0}$ setup employed here.

To highlight the role of scattering by comparison, we also show the evolution of an identical wave, but without any scattering from micro-instabilities (dashed lines). The most obvious difference between the two waves is that the pressure anisotropy is not permitted to exceed the instability thresholds when micro-instability scattering is included, while it is allowed to exceed the thresholds freely when micro-instability scattering is excluded. This demonstrates that some of the wave energy is indeed being thermalized when $\nu_{\rm eff}$ is active. The consequences of that thermalization can be seen in the slight damping of $\delta\rho$ (as compared to the $\nu_{\rm eff}=0$ wave). Notably, viscous damping due to micro-instability scattering begins immediately, unlike in figure 2 where appreciable damping occurs only near $k_{x}=0$ . This agrees with the expectation that viscous damping can occur even when the wavevector is not aligned with the magnetic-field direction. That said, the pressure anisotropy is not driven unstable when $|k_{x}|\lesssim k_{y}$ —a consequence of action conservation lowering the amplitude of the wave near the swing time. Therefore, in the spiral fast wave shown here, micro-instability scattering is not driven during the same period when Landau/Barnes damping is most effective, allowing the two effects to supplement each other (as opposed to $\nu_{\rm eff}$ exclusively suppressing Landau/Barnes damping). This result is, however, dependent on the initial wave amplitude and $\beta$ ; an increase in either of those quantities may cause the wave $\Delta p$ to reach the thresholds even at low $|k_{x}|$ . To explore this possibility, we now study the problem for varying $\beta$ and wave amplitudes.
