Furthermore, because the wave possesses low $k_{y}$ , it is sheared (and therefore damped) for fewer wave periods than a comparable wave at larger $k_{y}$ . Accordingly, the rate of damping has decreased to near zero and $\rm T\rightarrow 1$ . 66 6 At even higher values of $\beta$ ,it may be that the plasma behaves close enough to ideal MHD that the coupling between non-axisymmetric MRI and spiral density waves is recovered, as in Mamatsashvili et al. (2026). We leave such a possibility to future work.

In summary, self-generated micro-instability scattering leads to viscous damping that increases with the amplitude of the spiral density wave; however, the increase in damping is subtle, and when wave amplitudes approach nonlinear values ( $\delta u_{x,0}\sim 0.2v_{\rm th,i}$ ) this trend reverses for $\beta\gtrsim 50$ as the plasma mimics a strongly collisional fluid.

### 3.2 Turbulent Background Magnetic Field

We have so far studied the damping of spiral density waves in a uniform, azimuthal magnetic field, including when scattering from pressure-anisotropy-driven micro-instabilities is absent or active. Because there is no turbulence in this laminar background state, and therefore no vorticity, these studies allow us to probe only the damping and propagation of spiral density waves, not their excitation. Let us now consider a situation in which turbulence is also present in the shearing sheet, which allows us to address the propagation, damping, and excitation of spiral density waves. The requisite turbulence is assumed to be driven by the magnetorotational instability and/or the closely related magnetoviscous instability (unique to collisionless and weakly collisional differential flows; Quataert et al. 2002; Balbus 2004). This turbulent state implies that there is also a near-volume-filling, nonzero $\nu_{\rm eff}$ that results from micro-instabilities being driven by the turbulent pressure anisotropy. We now develop a set of equations to describe spiral waves in this turbulent system.

Unfortunately, deriving a numerically integrable, linearized KMHD system for spiral waves in a highly turbulent magnetic field is too onerous a task for this work. However, in the presence of sufficient scattering from micro-instabilities we may employ the Braginskii-MHD closure for $\Delta p$ , which makes it easier to obtain a tractable system of equations. The use of Braginskii-MHD requires scattering that is strong enough to maintain $\Delta p\ll p$ , which is normally satisfied by linear wave dynamics when $\nu_{\rm eff}\gg kv_{\rm th,i}$ . Physically, this criterion states that a particle must be scattered several times before it transits one wavelength, in order to ensure that the distribution does not drift far from LTE. In our system, tangling of the magnetic field by the turbulence effectively increases the path length that a field-following particle must travel in order to traverse one wavelength of the actual spiral wave. Due to this increased path length, particles can experience more scattering per wavelength transit than they would otherwise in a uniform field, so we expect $\nu_{\rm eff}\gtrsim kv_{\rm th,i}$ to be a sufficient condition in practice. To determine $\nu_{\rm eff}$ , equation (2) requires an estimate for $|3\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$:$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}|$ in this turbulent-field configuration. Because the magnetic field is no longer purely azimuthal, the sheared flow $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}=2Ax\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ now makes a nonzero contribution to $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$:$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}$ . Given that $|\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}|$ =1, the root-mean-square value of $|3\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$:$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}|$ will be ${\sim}|A|$ . We insert this root-mean-square estimate for the rate of strain into (2), finding that scattering is driven at a rate $\nu_{\rm eff}\sim\beta|A|$ ( ${\sim}\beta\Omega$ for Keplerian rotation, neglecting order-unity factors).77 7 The scattering rate $\nu_{\rm eff}$ is also perturbed by the wave-generated pressure anisotropy, as in §3.1.2. However, the wave contribution to $\nu_{\rm eff}$ (20) is proportional to the spiral-wave amplitude, which is small relative to that of the turbulence. Additionally, although these instabilities are not driven everywhere in the domain at a given instant, Arzamasskiy et al. (2023) found that they intermittently occupy each part of the domain sufficiently well that Braginskii-MHD is valid on (volumetric) average. Braginskii-MHD is therefore a valid assumption when $\beta\Omega\gtrsim kv_{\rm th,i}$ , or, in terms of the scale height $H\equiv c_{\rm s}/\Omega$ , $\beta\gtrsim kH$ (where $c_{\rm s}=\sqrt{5p/3\rho}$ is the adiabatic sound speed). Because spiral waves are excited near $k\sim k_{y}\sim H^{-1}$ (H&P), $\beta\gtrsim kH$ translates into the requirement that $\beta\gtrsim 1$ shortly after excitation (when $|k_{x}|\lesssim|k_{y}|$ ), but it eventually requires $\beta\gtrsim|k_{x}/k_{y}|$ long after excitation (once $|k_{x}|\gg|k_{y}|$ ).

Given the above assumptions, we may begin shaping the Braginskii-MHD equations into a linearized, solvable system. We first re-write the shearing-sheet momentum equation in a form that is more convenient with which to work:

$$ \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+2Ax\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right)\rho\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}=-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}p-2\Omega\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\rho\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}-2A\rho\delta u_{x}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\bm{\mathsf{T}}, $$

where $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}$ has been separated out of the bulk flow, viz. $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}=\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}+2Ax\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ . $\bm{\mathsf{T}}$ is a tensor that captures all nonlinear contributions to the perturbed momentum $\rho\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}$ , namely, the Reynolds, Maxwell, and viscous stresses:

$$ \bm{\mathsf{T}}=-\frac{\mbox{\boldmath{$BB$}}}{4\pi}+\bm{\mathsf{I}}\frac{B^{2}}{8\pi}+\rho\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}-\left(\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}-\frac{1}{3}\bm{\mathsf{I}}\right)\Delta p. $$

Because we now have turbulence, spiral waves, and a sheared flow present in the shearing sheet, but seek only to model the spiral waves and their interaction with the sheared flow, in what follows it is prudent to differentiate turbulent quantities from wave and sheared-flow quantities. We distinguish their contributions to each fluid variable by introducing the subscripts “ws” and “tu”, which are short for “wave and sheared flow” and “turbulence”. In “ws” quantities, we group the spiral-wave and sheared-flow contributions to the fluid variables together according to a shared property: none of them depend on the $z$ coordinate. The uniform parts of the density and pressure are therefore also contained within $\rho_{\rm ws}$ and $p_{\rm ws}$ , respectively. By contrast, “tu” quantities, which refer to fluctuations resulting from the turbulence, vary randomly with the $z$ coordinate. It is therefore implied that when fluid quantities are averaged over the $z$ coordinate, e.g., $\left\langle{\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}}\right\rangle_{z}$ , that the turbulent component vanishes, leaving only the “ws” component ( $\left\langle{\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}}\right\rangle_{z}=\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}$ ). Furthermore, $\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}=\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}-\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{0}$ contains only the wave perturbation to the flow, unlike $\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}$ , which contains the wave and turbulence contributions, but not the sheared flow. We make use of these properties in the calculations that follow.

With the “ws” and “tu” decomposition of the fluid properties, the contributions to the pressure anisotropy can be separated out as

$$ \Delta p=\Delta p_{\rm tu}+\Delta p_{\rm ws}\approx\Delta p_{\rm tu}+3\frac{p_{\rm ws}}{\nu_{\rm eff}}\left(\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}-\frac{1}{3}\bm{\mathsf{I}}\right)\,\mbox{\boldmath{$:$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}, $$

where we have left the turbulent pressure anisotropy ( $\Delta p_{\rm tu}$ ) as-is for brevity. We emphasize that, in the “ws” contribution to equation (23), pressure anisotropy is driven by both the wave and the sheared flow (as opposed to being driven by the wave perturbation alone, like in §3.1.2), because the “ws” velocity $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}$ includes $2Ax\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}$ and the magnetic field is not purely azimuthal.

We can now isolate the evolution of the spiral waves by performing a $z$ -average of the dynamical equations. If the magnetic field is isotropically tangled by the turbulence, then the $z$ -averaged viscous stress becomes:

$$ \left\langle{\bm{\mathsf{T}}_{\Delta p}}\right\rangle_{z}=-\left\langle{\left(\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}-\frac{1}{3}\bm{\mathsf{I}}\right)\Delta p}\right\rangle_{z}\approx-\left\langle{\left(\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}-\frac{1}{3}\bm{\mathsf{I}}\right)\Delta p_{\rm tu}}\right\rangle_{z}-\left[\frac{p_{\rm ws}}{5\nu_{\rm eff}}\left(\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}+(\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws})^{\mathsf{T}}-\frac{2}{3}\bm{\mathsf{I}}\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}\right)\right]. $$

To understand how we arrived at the final term in this expression, first recall that the averaging passes through $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}$ and $p_{\rm ws}$ . Then, when equation (23) is inserted into equation (22) and averaged, one need only determine $\langle\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\rangle_{z}$ and $\langle\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\rangle_{z}$ to find the wave/background part of the viscous stress. Borrowing from the linear treatment of magneto-elastic waves in tangled-field configurations and studies of the turbulent dynamo (Moffatt, 1985; Malyshkin & Kulsrud, 2002; Hosking et al., 2020, e.g.,), we assume that, given many uncorrelated fluctuations over the $z$ dimension, $\langle\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\rangle_{z}$ and $\langle\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\rangle_{z}$ are isotropic, unity-trace tensors. For tensors of rank 2 and 4, these are $\frac{1}{3}\delta_{ij}$ and $\frac{1}{15}(\delta_{ij}\delta_{nm}+\delta_{in}\delta_{jm}+\delta_{im}\delta_{nj})$ respectively. The resultant viscous stress is then equivalent to the isotropic value suppressed by a factor of 5 (Malyshkin & Kulsrud, 2002; Gruzinov, 2002; Gruzinov, 2006).

With the tangled-field viscous stress estimated, we may address the remainder of the momentum equation. In equation (21), the terms containing $\left\langle{\rho\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}}\right\rangle_{z}$ are simplified further by noting that we are already limited to the large- $\beta$ regime, where density fluctuations from MRI turbulence satisfy $\delta\rho\ll\rho_{0}$ (Salvesen et al., 2016). Accordingly, given the assumed linearity of the spiral waves themselves, $\left\langle{\rho\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}}\right\rangle_{z}\approx\rho_{0}\left\langle{\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}}\right\rangle_{z}=\rho_{0}\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}$ . In all, the averaged momentum equation becomes

$$ \rho_{0}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+2Ax\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right)\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}\approx-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}p_{\rm ws}-2\rho_{0}\Omega\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\delta\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}-2A\rho_{0}\delta u_{x,\rm ws}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$y$}}}+\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\left[\frac{p_{\rm ws}}{5\nu_{\rm eff}}\left(\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}+(\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws})^{\mathsf{T}}-\frac{2}{3}\bm{\mathsf{I}}\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm ws}\right)\right]+\left\langle{\mathcal{N}}\right\rangle_{z}. $$

In (25), we have separated out the “tu” viscous stress from equation (24), and gathered it with the remaining nonlinear stresses in equation (22) into a term denoted by $\mathcal{N}$ (following H&P’s notation). In Heinemann & Papaloizou (2009b), the authors used ideal MHD simulations of MRI turbulence to demonstrate that the averaged nonlinearity $\left\langle{\mathcal{N}}\right\rangle_{z}$ is negligible in comparison to all density-wave contributions to the momentum equation. The role of $\left\langle{\mathcal{N}}\right\rangle_{z}$ may be even weaker in this work: Majeski & Kunz (2024) showed that Alfvénic motions (such as the MRI) interact weakly with compressive dynamics (such as spiral density waves) in high- $\beta$ , collisionless plasmas. Motivated by these results, we neglect $\left\langle{\mathcal{N}}\right\rangle_{z}$ henceforth.

The only equation remaining to be determined is the evolution equation for the wave-driven isotropic pressure, for which we use (9). It might seem that we can once again apply the same averaging procedure to (9) that was used to obtain (25). However, doing so would incorrectly overestimate the tangled-field heat flux. In the presence of a tangled magnetic field, the heat flux is suppressed by the longer path length that particles must travel in order to transport heat from one location to another. According to Malyshkin (2001), this suppression is proportional to the square of the ratio of the magnetic-field correlation length to the temperature-gradient scale, the latter being equivalent to the spiral-wave wavelength, ${\sim}2\pi H$ . Collisionless MRI simulations indicate that the magnetic field is correlated on scales smaller than $H$ (Kunz et al., 2016, cf. figure 3 of), so we expect the heat flux to be suppressed beyond the $\langle\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\rangle=1/5$ amount by an additional factor $\gtrsim 4\pi^{2}$ . Given such strong suppression, the heat fluxes may be neglected entirely; therefore, the isotropic pressure approximately follows the ideal adiabatic relation ${\rm d}/{\rm d}t(p/\rho^{5/3})=0$ .88 8 Even if the parallel heat flux were not suppressed by the additional tangling factor, its primary consequence for spiral-wave evolution would be to smear out temperature fluctuations and enforce an isothermal pressure relation. Including a strong, isotropic heat flux in our calculations does not increase wave damping to the degree that observations would be affected.

We now use the adiabatic relation to eliminate $p_{\rm ws}$ , and insert the assumption of linear, shearing waveforms (10) into (25) (with $\left\langle{\mathcal{N}}\right\rangle_{z}$ dropped) and the continuity equation to find a system of ODEs that is readily integrable numerically:

$$ \frac{{\rm d}\delta u_{x,\rm ws}}{{\rm d}t}=-{\rm i}\left(k_{x}(t)+\frac{2A}{5\nu_{\rm eff}}k_{y}\right)c_{\rm s}^{2}\frac{\delta\rho_{\rm ws}}{\rho_{0}}+2\Omega\delta u_{y,\rm ws}-\frac{p_{0}}{5\rho_{0}\nu_{\rm eff}}\left(\frac{4}{3}k_{x}(t)^{2}\delta u_{x,\rm ws}+k_{y}^{2}\delta u_{x,\rm ws}+\frac{1}{3}k_{y}k_{x}(t)\delta u_{y,\rm ws}\right), \frac{{\rm d}\delta u_{y,\rm ws}}{{\rm d}t}=-{\rm i}\left(k_{y}+\frac{2A}{5\nu_{\rm eff}}k_{x}(t)\right)c_{\rm s}^{2}\frac{\delta\rho_{\rm ws}}{\rho_{0}}-2(A+\Omega)\delta u_{x,\rm ws}-\frac{p_{0}}{5\rho_{0}\nu_{\rm eff}}\left(\frac{4}{3}k_{y}^{2}\delta u_{y,\rm ws}+k_{x}(t)^{2}\delta u_{y,\rm ws}+\frac{1}{3}k_{y}k_{x}(t)\delta u_{x,\rm ws}\right), \frac{{\rm d}\delta\rho_{\rm ws}}{{\rm d}t}=-{\rm i}k_{y}\rho_{0}\delta u_{y,\rm ws}-{\rm i}k_{x}(t)\rho_{0}\delta u_{x,\rm ws}. $$

Because of the assumptions of isotropic tangling and weak nonlinearity, we no longer have any direct contribution from the magnetic field. In the absence of rotation and shear then, the waves described by the system (26) become indistinguishable from viscously damped acoustic waves. For this reason, we refer to the spiral density waves in this section as acoustic waves rather than fast waves. We make this distinction solely for the purpose of emphasizing the dominant physics at play, since, in the high- $\beta$ limit, fast waves and hydrodynamic acoustic waves are closely related. We are also only concerned with the “wave and sheared flow” fluid quantities now, so the subscript “ws” is dropped henceforth.

In the next three sections, we present solutions to the system (26) for initially leading spiral waves (§3.2.1, as a parallel study to §3.1.1 and §3.1.2). We then discuss the physics involved in the excitation and damping of spiral waves that are converted from vorticity fluctuations (§3.2.2), and finally numerically solve for the full evolution of converted spiral waves as a direct, collisionless analog to the process described by H&P (§3.2.3).

#### 3.2.1 Initial Acoustic Wave Solutions

To isolate the effects of viscous damping due to a background turbulent $\nu_{\rm eff}$ on the propagation of spiral density waves alone, we first perform an analogous study to §3.1.1 and §3.1.2. As in those sections, we numerically integrate the system (26) for the evolution of a leading acoustic wave, which is initialized as a leading perturbation to $u_{x}$ alone and is evolved from $k_{x}=-10k_{y}$ to $k_{x}=10k_{y}$ . The scattering rate, motivated in §3.2, is set to $\nu_{\rm eff}=(3/4)\beta\Omega$ .

*Figure 6: Leading to trailing transfer coefficient for spiral waves in a turbulent background magnetic field, assuming $\nu_{\rm eff}=(3/4)\beta\Omega$ . Moderate $\beta$ waves are most strongly damped because the viscosity is proportional to $\beta^{-1}$ . In the high- $\beta$ limit, waves propagate undamped as they would in an ideal MHD plasma. Note the different axis limits from earlier figures, which ensure that we do not violate the assumptions of Braginskii-MHD. The dashed line represents the WKB prediction for $\rm T=0.1$ obtained via (28).*

Figure 6 shows the transfer coefficient $\rm T$ for this acoustic spiral density wave, given the same definition (19) employed in §3.1. Here, the range of $\beta$ values begins at 10, which is equivalent to the ratio $|k_{x}|/k_{y}$ at the start of the simulation (to ensure the scattering-rate condition for the use of Braginskii-MHD is met).99 9 The Braginskii requirement $\beta\Omega\gtrsim kv_{\rm th,i}$ is technically violated in the top left corner of figure 6, however we stress that the waves are already strongly damped before one gets to such high $k_{y}c_{\rm s}/\Omega$ at $\beta=10$ . In all other regions of figure 6, $\beta\Omega\gtrsim kv_{\rm th,i}$ is satisfied by the density waves. For the parameter range shown in figure 6, significant amounts of damping occur for spiral density waves at moderately large values of the plasma $\beta$ , even for waves with low azimuthal wavenumber. As $\beta$ increases however, the scattering rate grows and the viscosity vanishes, leading to virtually undamped waves in the very high- $\beta$ , low- $k_{y}$ portion of the plot. Physically, this high- $\beta$ limit is one in which the scattering rate has grown to far exceed the wave frequency, which itself is independent of $\beta$ given the assumptions of §3.2. Accordingly, at such high $\nu_{\rm eff}$ , the pressure anisotropy becomes very small, and the viscous damping with it.

To better understand the dependence of the transfer coefficient in figure 6 through analytic means, we can employ an identical WKB approach to that used in §3.1.1. Once again, we assume that the magnitude of the shear $|A|$ is small, in this case $\ll k_{y}c_{\rm s}$ , where $v_{\rm th,i}$ has been replaced by $c_{\rm s}$ as the characteristic wave speed. Given the slow evolution of $k$ that follows from this assumption, the waves approximately satisfy the instantaneous dispersion relation at a given $k$ :

$$ \omega^{3}+\frac{7{\rm i}}{25}\left(\frac{k^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}}{\nu_{\rm eff}}\right)\omega^{2}-\left[k^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}+4\Omega^{2}+\frac{12}{625}\frac{c_{\rm s}^{4}}{\nu_{\rm eff}^{2}}\left(k_{x}^{4}+\frac{4}{3}k_{y}^{2}k_{x}^{2}+k_{y}^{4}\right)\right]\omega-\frac{3{\rm i}}{25}\frac{k^{4}c_{\rm s}^{4}}{\nu_{\rm eff}}=0. $$

Because (27) is only third order, the solutions can be obtained exactly, however their full forms are too cumbersome with which to work. Fortunately, the requirement $\nu_{\rm eff}\gtrsim kv_{\rm th,i}\sim kc_{\rm s}$ inherent to Braginskii-MHD guarantees that the damping rate of these acoustic waves will always be small compared to the real part of their frequency, so we once again use the expansion (14) to approximate the real and imaginary parts of the acoustic wave frequency with (15), finding:

$$ \omega_{r}\approx\pm k_{y}c_{\rm s}\sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}}+\frac{4\Omega^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}}+\frac{12k_{y}^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}}{625\nu_{\rm eff}^{2}}\left(\frac{k^{4}}{k_{y}^{4}}+\frac{4k_{x}^{2}}{3k_{y}^{2}}\right)}, \omega_{i}\approx-\frac{7k_{y}^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}}{50\nu_{\rm eff}}\left(\frac{k^{2}}{k_{y}^{2}}\right)+\frac{3k_{y}^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}}{50\nu_{\rm eff}}\left(\frac{k^{4}}{k_{y}^{4}}\right)\frac{k_{y}^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}}{\omega_{r}^{2}}. $$

Given $\Delta p\ll p$ and the corresponding assumption of weak viscosity, the final term in the square root of (28a) must be small compared to the others. Furthermore, if we assume Keplerian rotation with $\Omega=\frac{4}{3}|A|$ , then the assumption $|A|\ll k_{y}c_{\rm s}$ reduces (28a) to the simple acoustic wave frequency $\omega_{r}=\pm kc_{\rm s}$ , as expected. When $\omega_{r}^{2}=k^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}$ is substituted into (28b), we obtain $\omega_{i}\approx-2k^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}/(25\nu_{\rm eff})$ . Given $k_{x}(t)=-(10+2At)k_{y}$ and Keplerian shear, we approximate the results of figure 6 by evaluating the integral (18) with this $\omega_{i}$ from $t=0$ until $k_{x}(t)=-10k_{y}$ to obtain ${\rm T}\approx\exp[-48k_{y}^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}/(\beta\Omega^{2})]$ . We plot the curve that this approximation predicts for $\rm T=0.1$ as a dashed line in figure 6. The agreement between the numerical and analytic solutions indicates that the lowest-order WKB approximation is effective for capturing the damping of these spiral acoustic waves, and that this agreement holds even when $|A|\sim k_{y}c_{\rm s}$ .

#### 3.2.2 Expectations: Initial Vortical Wave

The previous sections have investigated the propagation and damping of collisionless spiral waves initialized as leading fast/acoustic waves. However, the actual process expected to occur in accretion flows involves their swing-induced excitation from fluctuations in the vorticity (§1.1; H&P, Chagelishvili et al. (1997)). If we wish to make an effective prediction about observable properties of spiral density waves in non-LTE accretion flows, we must probe the excitation of these waves as well. Before finding numerical solutions for this process, however, let us first consider some of the changes that occur to the governing equations described in H&P as a result of micro-instability-induced viscosity.

In their work, H&P found that static fluctuations in the pseudo-potential vorticity (PPV),

$$ \xi\equiv\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\rho u_{y})-\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\rho u_{x})-2(A+\Omega)\rho, $$

which resemble static entropy waves (also known as vortical waves), excite acoustic waves when they undergo a swing. It can be shown that, in the absence of viscosity, the pseudo-potential vorticity is conserved by the system (26). This, in turn, implies that there is no mechanism in the ideal linearized equations to produce the requisite vortical waves (H&P). When including the turbulent nonlinearities that were dropped to obtain (26), however, Heinemann & Papaloizou (2009b) demonstrated that $\xi$ grows slowly compared to the vertical sound crossing time ( $H/c_{\rm s}$ ) due to the underlying MRI turbulence. Therefore, turbulence slowly builds up fluctuations in the PPV, which are otherwise conserved, so that they eventually swing and are converted into spiral density waves.

In the collisionless, turbulent system we describe with (26), the PPV is no longer conserved. Using (26) to calculate the evolution equation for fluctuations in the PPV, $\delta\xi\approx\rho_{0}\partial_{x}u_{y}-\rho_{0}\partial_{y}u_{x}-2(A+\Omega)\delta\rho$ , we find that

$$ \frac{{\rm d}\delta\xi}{{\rm d}t}=\frac{2Ap_{0}}{3\rho_{0}\nu_{\rm eff}}\left(k^{2}_{x}(t)-k_{y}^{2}\right)\delta\rho-\frac{p_{0}k^{2}(t)}{5\rho_{0}\nu_{\rm eff}}\bigl[\delta\xi+2(A-\Omega)\delta\rho\bigr]. $$

At $|k_{x}(t)|\gg|k_{y}|$ , PPV fluctuations, or vortical waves, possess negligible $\delta\rho/\rho_{0}$ , so according to (30) their primary behavior is simply to damp. This is also true when the shear is small. By neglecting the highest-order terms in $|A|/k_{y}c_{\rm s}\sim\Omega/k_{y}c_{\rm s}\ll 1$ and inserting our approximation for $\nu_{\rm eff}$ , we integrate equation (30) directly from an initial (negative) $k_{x,0}$ and $\delta\xi_{0}$ to obtain an estimate of the decay of the vortical wave as it approaches the swing (for Keplerian shear):

$$ \delta\xi(t)\approx\delta\xi_{0}\exp\left[-\frac{8}{75}\frac{k_{y}^{2}c_{\rm s}^{2}}{\beta\Omega^{2}}\left(\frac{k_{x}(t)-k_{x,0}}{k_{y}}+\frac{k^{3}_{x}(t)-k_{x,0}^{3}}{3k_{y}^{3}}\right)\right]. $$

Therefore, not only does viscosity damp spiral waves after excitation, it also affects the buildup of vorticity that is necessary for density-wave excitation in the first place. With (26) being a linear set of equations, the amplitude of the excited density wave is proportional to the amplitude of $\delta\xi$ when $k_{x}(t)=0$ (H&P). So, assuming initially tightly wound vortical modes ( $|k_{x,0}|\gtrsim 3k_{y}\sim 3H^{-1}$ , so that the cubic term in (31) dominates), we predict that the excitation of spiral density waves is suppressed by a factor $\gtrsim{\rm e}$ whenever

$$ \beta\lesssim|k_{x,0}/k_{y}|^{3}/10. $$

Seeing as our Braginskii approximation is valid only when $\beta\gtrsim|k_{x,0}/k_{y}|$ , the smallest value of $\beta$ for which we can reliably predict excitation to be suppressed is $\beta_{\rm min}{\approx}3$ . We emphasize, however, that (32) includes only dissipation incurred prior to the swing, and spiral waves may be suppressed down to $\beta{\sim}1$ due to damping that occurs after the swing.

There is also the matter of how vortical-acoustic wave conversion (and therefore density wave excitation) occurs in a viscous system. To develop a qualitative understanding of this process, let us probe the linear dispersion relation (27), which reveals the relationship between the acoustic- and vortical-wave branches. In figure 7 we plot all (vortical and acoustic) exact solutions to (27) for two values of $\beta$ (10 and 100) and $k_{y}c_{\rm s}=\Omega$ .

*Figure 7: Solutions of the dispersion relation of shearing waves in an isotropically tangled magnetic field, for $0<|k_{x}|<10k_{y}$ at $\beta=10$ and $100$ . In each case, the vortical wave is the branch with no real frequency, while the acoustic spiral wave solutions have a real frequency that is much larger than their damping rate at all wavenumbers. Note the apparent linear dependence of damping rate on $\beta^{-1}$ , which explains the variation of $\rm T$ seen in figure 6.*

The color on each branch corresponds to the value of $|k_{x}/k_{y}|$ for which the solution was obtained, the horizontal axis corresponds to its real frequency, and the vertical axis to its damping rate. In the spiral wave excitation process, we begin at the bottom of the $\omega_{r}=0$ vortical wave branch with a leading wave satisfying $|k_{x}|\gg|k_{y}|$ . As the wave shears, $|k_{x}|$ decreases and the wave moves upwards along the dispersion branch, which in turn slows the rate of damping. Eventually, when the wave swings ( $k_{x}=0$ ), the dispersion relations of the vortical wave and the acoustic waves nearly converge. It is at this point where near-resonance is achieved between the acoustic and vortical waves, allowing energy to be exchanged between the coupled branches in a process often referred to as “linear mode conversion” (Friedland et al., 1987; Hinkel-Lipsker et al., 1992; Tracy & Kaufman, 1993, see, e.g.,). After the swing, when $|k_{x}|$ begins to increase, the newly generated acoustic wave grows both in frequency and damping rate, yielding a trailing spiral density wave, which, when considering damping that has occurred throughout this conversion process, is lower in amplitude than it would be if viscosity were absent. By comparing the vertical axes limits at $\beta=10$ and $\beta=100$ , we see that the damping rate is inversely proportional to $\beta$ , or alternatively, linearly proportional to magnetic energy density. This is no surprise given that the effective viscosity in our micro-unstable plasma is $\mu_{\rm eff}\equiv p/\nu_{\rm eff}\propto B^{2}/\Omega$ .

The choice of smaller initial $|k_{x}|$ is made here to enable us to explore values of $\beta$ down to 5, while not violating the assumptions of Braginskii-MHD. In figure 8(a), the numerical solutions for $\delta\rho(t)$ are provided for $\beta\in[5,100]$ , with $k_{y}c_{\rm s}=\Omega$ and $\nu_{\rm eff}=(3/4)\beta\Omega$ . The tick marks in the color scale correspond to the exact values of $\beta$ for the solutions given.

The dotted line tracks the peak $k_{y}$ for excitation as a function of $\beta$ . Viscous damping leads to a skew of the peak excitation wavenumber toward smaller $k_{y}$ at moderate $\beta$ . At very high $\beta$ , the peak $k_{y}$ settles near the ${\sim}H^{-1}$ prediction of H&P because the viscosity is microphysically regulated to very small values. As a result, non-LTE spiral waves at moderate $\beta$ , such as those likely to arise in low-luminosity accretion flows, feature lower amplitudes and azimuthal wavenumbers than their ideal-MHD counterparts (approximated here by the asymptotically high- $\beta$ limit).*

In figure 8, we only studied waves with $k_{y}=H^{-1}$ , because wavenumbers near this value were predicted by H&P to be excited at the largest amplitudes. However, it is worth probing whether this remains the case in the presence of viscous damping. H&P demonstrated that, although the excited wave amplitudes peak near $k_{y}\sim H^{-1}$ , there is a finite width to the distribution of excited wavenumbers that extends symmetrically to higher and lower $k_{y}$ . In the collisionless system, viscous damping preferentially damps large- $k_{y}$ waves (because the ratio of their shear time to wave period, and therefore damping time, is longer). This preference should induce an asymmetry in excited wave amplitudes that skews the distribution to lower $k_{y}$ . Given the dependence of the damping strength on $\beta$ , this skew should become more prominent with decreasing $\beta$ .

In Figure 9, we test these expectations by initializing leading vortical waves with $k_{x,0}=-10k_{y}$ , and evolving them through the conversion process until the wavenumber is reversed ( $k_{x,0}=10k_{y}$ ). Rather than initializing a fixed $\delta u_{y}$ , here we initialize a fixed PPV fluctuation, $\delta\xi=0.01\rho_{0}\Omega$ . This choice is motivated by Heinemann & Papaloizou (2009b), where the authors found that at low $k_{y}c_{\rm s}/\Omega$ the spectrum of PPV supplied by MRI turbulence is approximately flat. The shading in figure 9 shows the final peak-to-peak amplitude of the resulting spiral density wave given the (fixed) initial PPV perturbation. At moderate $\beta$ ( $\lesssim 30$ ), where damping is stronger, the distribution of excited wave amplitudes is not only decreased all around, but skewed toward lower $k_{y}$ as expected. The dotted line tracks the $k_{y}$ of the most strongly excited wave at each $\beta$ , finding that at $\beta=10$ the peak azimuthal wavenumber is lower than the MHD equivalent (which is effectively the same as $\beta\gtrsim 10^{3}$ in figure 9) by a factor $\gtrsim 2$ . Importantly, however, this result is dependent on the initial ratio $|k_{x,0}/k_{y}|$ : the peak $k_{y}$ for excitation can be decreased further by initializing a leading vortical wave with a larger value of $|k_{x,0}/k_{y}|$ , so that the wave has more time to damp before and after the swing. Alternatively, the low- $k_{y}$ skew can be weakened by initializing a wave with $|k_{x,0}|\lesssim|k_{y}|$ . In H&P, the authors seeded $\delta\xi$ at values of $|k_{x,0}/k_{y}|$ that were so large ( ${\sim}100$ ) that the vortical waves would damp entirely prior to the swing time in the viscous framework studied here. Whether such radial leading waves are the most accurate choice for the turbulent source of $\xi$ is presently unclear. Therefore, for precise predictions of the change in the dominant $k_{y}$ at which spiral density waves are excited, $|k_{x,0}/k_{y}|$ for the PPV fluctuations will have to be constrained using future collisionless accretion-flow turbulence simulations.

## 4 Discussion: Observational and Modeling Implications

Spiral density waves are predicted to play a significant role in determining the morphology and amplitude of fluctuations in the emission region of a black-hole accretion flow. We have demonstrated that the excitation and propagation of spiral density waves in collisionless plasmas can be suppressed. This finding has consequences for accretion-flow observables across a broad range of low-luminosity systems, including those relevant to the EHT project. There are, of course, many plasma-independent effects that determine the actual appearance of black-hole images and mock observations from GRMHD simulations (EHT et al., 2022b). We therefore do not make any precise statements here about what the exact light curve variabilities or visibility amplitudes should be from accretion-flow observations. We can, however, make predictions about how such observations ought to differ from those predicted by GRMHD simulations without Landau/Barnes damping or microphysically regulated viscous stresses.

We first consider the amplitude of the spiral density waves, which we associated with non-axisymmetric fluctuations in emitted synchrotron power near the black-hole event horizon. We find that spiral density wave amplitudes are significantly suppressed by viscous stresses at moderately large values of the plasma $\beta$ ( $\in[3,30]$ ). Given the potential role of density waves in determining the variability of accretion-flow emission, such damping may have important observational consequences. In particular, the absence of non-LTE damping mechanisms in GRMHD models may help explain why the EHT library, on average, overestimated the variability of Sgr A∗.1010 10 Certain models of the Sgr A∗ accretion flow, referred to as “magnetically arrested” (Igumenshchev et al., 2003; Narayan et al., 2003; Tchekhovskoy et al., 2011, MAD;), are often characterized as being low $\beta$ ( $\beta<1$ ). One might therefore conclude that these models fall outside of the range of $\beta$ in which we predict significant suppression of spiral waves ( $\beta\in[3,30]$ ). However, in such models the low- $\beta$ state is achieved close to the Sgr A∗ event horizon, and beyond ${\sim}10\,r_{g}$ the plasma $\beta$ can grow to be $>1$ (Dhruv et al., 2025). Because spiral waves are thought to originate outside the emission region (Conroy et al., 2025), which itself is constrained to be within ${\sim}5\,r_{g}$ (EHT et al., 2022a), spiral-wave suppression may be significant even in MAD models of the Sgr A∗ accretion flow. Thus far, only one global investigation of weakly collisional accretion has been performed with the goal of modeling Sgr A∗ (Dhruv et al., 2025), and their results indicate that variability is indeed reduced in the presence of viscous dissipation. In their case, the observed decrease in variability was modest, however this may be a consequence of the fact that they assumed there was an additional (non-micro-instability driven) source of scattering present everywhere in addition to that which results from micro-instabilities. Any additional scattering reduces the impact of viscous-damping effects on spiral density waves (given that the viscosity goes as $\mu_{\rm eff}\propto\nu_{\rm eff}^{-1}$ ), and therefore limits the reduction in variability. We therefore predict that a truly collisionless approach with a self-consistent treatment of micro-instability scattering will feature weaker spiral density waves and a further reduction in variability. This is, in fact, already supported by earlier simulation results studying MRI turbulence using a hybrid-kinetic shearing-box approach (Kunz et al., 2016), which naturally captures the exact scattering rate of micro-instabilities because the instabilities and the particles they scatter are simulated directly. In their simulation, which possessed $\langle\beta^{-1}\rangle\sim 0.15$ , large-scale trailing density waves were nearly absent, only being detectable after vertical averaging, and even then having amplitudes $\delta\rho/\rho\lesssim 0.05$ (see their fig. 4). By comparison, the density waves seen in the MHD simulations of Heinemann & Papaloizou (2009b) had amplitudes ${\approx}4$ times larger. The suppression that Kunz et al. (2016) measured in spiral-density-wave amplitudes may also have been reinforced by the fact that, at such low $\beta$ , the peak $y$ -wavelength for density wave excitation could have been stretched beyond the box length that they employed in the azimuthal direction ( $L_{y}=4H$ ).

Another implication of this work concerns EHT observations that are yet to come: emission-region pattern speeds (Conroy et al., 2023). Improvements to the EHT will soon make it possible to construct movies of the accretion flows around Sgr A∗ and M87∗ (Doeleman et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2019). Given the asymmetric emission already present in still frames of these sources, a time sequence of such images would reveal the movement of any non-axisymmetric features (more precisely their rotation). In movies generated from GRMHD simulations, it has been found that these patterns precess at a rate well below the Keplerian speed at their radius, in other words, the observed evolution is not the result of rigid rotation of a particular region of the flow. Instead, the frequency of this rotation has been shown to coincide with the pattern speed of spiral fast/acoustic waves, $\Omega_{\rm p}\equiv\Omega_{0}-\omega/m$ , where $m=k_{y}r_{0}$ is the azimuthal mode number, $\Omega_{0}$ is the orbital frequency at $r_{0}$ , and the negative sign on $\omega$ reflects the wave’s inward propagation (Conroy et al., 2023). It is therefore natural to question whether collisionless physics leads to new expectations for the $\Omega_{\rm p}$ of these spiral waves via changes to $m$ , $\omega$ , and $\Omega_{0}$ . Let us first consider changes in the azimuthal mode number $m$ . Given that $m$ is proportional to $k_{y}$ , figure 9 implies that lower values of $m$ are preferred by collisionless spiral density waves than are preferred by MHD ones. Assuming, for the moment, that the detected waves are excited at the same radius when viscosity is included as they are in its absence, we expect that GRMHD simulations overestimate the pattern speed of emission-region structures, and that they do so more significantly if the plasma $\beta$ is moderate or low. This statement does, however, rely heavily on the assumption that the region from which these spiral waves originate is unchanged by collisionless physics. Any such change will affect the orbital frequency at excitation $\Omega_{0}$ , which would directly modify the pattern speed. In MHD, the radius at which these waves are excited is set by a balance of several factors, including (but not limited to) where the production of vorticity is most efficient and how the wave amplitude changes with radius. We cannot address how these details might change due to collisionless effects in our limited analysis, so fully nonlinear simulations are necessary to resolve this area of uncertainty in our prediction of lower $\Omega_{\rm p}$ . As for the wave frequency $\omega$ , it too is determined by the radius of excitation. When moving with a wave packet inward toward the emission region, geometrical optics dictates that the wave frequency $\omega$ remains unchanged. Hence, the local properties of the flow at excitation, which depend on $r_{0}$ , determine $\omega$ . Lastly, it is also possible that, given strong viscous damping, spiral density waves become so low amplitude that they no longer dominate the morphology of the emission region. In this case, the above conclusion that pattern speeds should be overestimated by GRMHD would change entirely, instead simply becoming uncorrelated with spiral density wave excitation. Unfortunately, to address the consequences that possibility holds for the time evolution of black-hole emission, one needs to quantify all of the other potential sources of emission region variability, which is beyond the scope of this work.

## 5 Conclusion

We have presented an investigation of the excitation, propagation, and damping of spiral density waves in collisionless accretion-flow plasmas, in which we consider the roles played by a variety of non-LTE effects and physical setups. In a background magnetic field that is laminar and azimuthal, spiral density waves satisfying $k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}\gtrsim 10\Omega$ were found to be strongly suppressed by Landau/Barnes damping. Waves at lower $k_{y}$ , however, such as those most strongly excited by MRI turbulence ( $k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}\sim\Omega$ ), were nearly unaffected by Landau/Barnes damping. When scattering from wave-generated micro-instabilities was included, the resultant viscous damping increased spiral-wave dissipation, even at $k_{y}v_{\rm th,i}\sim\Omega$ . The strongest dissipation of spiral density waves was found to occur in a turbulent background magnetic-field configuration, where micro-instability scattering is primarily driven by the turbulence rather than the waves themselves. At moderately large values of $\beta$ ( $\in[3,30]$ ), we found that spiral density waves are not only viscously damped after excitation, but also that the turbulent fluctuations necessary to excite them in the first place can be suppressed. Given the importance of micro-instability scattering in damping spiral waves, we conclude that suppression is broadly expected to occur in high- $\beta$ accretion flow plasmas, but not low- $\beta$ ones. Furthermore, because spiral density waves perturb the the rate of synchrotron emission from the accreting plasma, these results are expected to impact observations of optically thin, low-luminosity accretion flows. Specifically, micro-instability-mediated viscous damping is predicted to reduce both emission variability and the pattern speed of emission-region features relative to corresponding LTE models. These results therefore demonstrate that micro-physical plasma processes can indirectly impact the observable structure of hot accretion flows, and advocate for future modeling efforts that employ well-motivated closures for non-LTE physics, so that tighter constraints may be placed on the parameter regimes of the accretion flows themselves.

Being a study of spiral density waves in the relatively isolated shearing sheet, there are obvious limitations to this work. Clearly, both general and special relativistic effects play an enormous role in determining the actual morphology of the emission region, at least given some underlying structure inherent to the plasma itself. It is most prudent, however, to consider those effects that we have neglected even in our local approximation to the entire spiral wave generation/propagation process. The most significant of these limitations is the neglect of nonlinear effects (beyond self-generated micro-instabilities). In reality, because spiral density waves are fast/acoustic waves, they are expected to steepen into shocks within roughly $t_{\rm shock}\sim(kc_{\rm s}\delta\rho/\rho_{0})^{-1}$ of being excited (Heinemann & Papaloizou, 2012; Majeski et al., 2023). This sets an effective upper limit on the amount of time during which such waves linearly damp. An order-of-magnitude estimate of this time, given $\delta\rho/\rho_{0}=0.1$ and $k_{x}\sim k_{y}$ , is $tk_{y}c_{\rm s}\sim 10$ after the swing time. From figure 8, it is clear that this is still enough time to see significant changes in the spiral wave amplitude from damping. Actual differences, however, may be even larger, because viscosity can slow steepening, and, if strong enough, may halt steepening altogether. Carefully designed nonlinear simulations will better constrain the additional differences that occur as a result of this discrepancy in steepening rates.

After the assumption of linearity, our treatment of the scattering rate is the next-most immediate area in which improvement could be made. In an analytic model, it is difficult to improve accuracy beyond the approach used here unless a multi-scale method can be developed that accurately describes the saturated state of the intermediate-scale MRI turbulence, and therefore its rate of strain. Given that MRI turbulence is an exceptionally active area of research and the general applicability of many such results is still under careful scrutiny, a simulation-based approach is more favorable. The two most physically realistic numerical approaches for such a problem would either be fully- or hybrid-kinetic (Riquelme et al., 2012; Hoshino, 2015; Kunz et al., 2016; Inchingolo et al., 2018; Sandoval et al., 2024), or a fluid-based approach employing the Chew-Goldberger-Low (CGL) equations (Sharma et al., 2006; Squire et al., 2017). The former options, although based on first principles, are computationally expensive, especially if substantial scale separation is desired not only between the spiral wave and the MRI turbulence, but also between the MRI turbulence and the ion-Larmor scale. The CGL fluid approach is much more affordable, but compromises on the accuracy of the heat fluxes, which above all, are responsible for Landau/Barnes damping. If spiral wave behavior is the primary goal, this may be an acceptable compromise, given that accurate viscous stresses are of greater concern to the damping of spiral density waves than Landau/Barnes damping. Nonetheless, the CGL model by itself does not accurately model the excitation and saturation of micro-instabilities, nor their feedback on $\Delta p$ , so a well-crafted closure must be employed that realizes the expected rate of scattering from (2).

Finally, in our derivation of the governing equations for shearing waves in a turbulent magnetic field, we made the simplifying assumption that the field is tangled isotropically. Realistic MRI turbulence, however, does not produce isotropically tangled magnetic fields. If it did, the stresses that drive angular momentum transport—a crucial ingredient of accretion—would be negligible (Balbus et al., 1994; Hawley et al., 1995; Brandenburg et al., 1996). Therefore, the equations provided here represent a limiting case of waves in extremely tangled fields. To relax this assumption of isotropy, modifications can be made to the approximations used for $\langle\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\rangle$ and $\langle\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\rangle$ . For $\langle\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\rangle$ , the $xy$ component of an updated prescription could be estimated from the Maxwell stress $\langle B_{x}B_{y}\rangle$ that is often reported in simulations (see, for example, the references to collisionless MRI turbulence cited throughout this work). Second-order correlations among other components of the magnetic field, however, are not often reported. Similarly, the fourth-order correlation, $\langle\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\rangle$ , is not closely related to any quantity that has yet been constrained in MRI turbulence simulations. These additional correlations can, however, be measured in future simulations of the collisionless MRI, enabling a straightforward $\mathcal{O}(1)$ update to the present work.

## Appendix A Derivation of the shearing sheet Kinetic MHD Equations

Here we present a derivation of the shearing-sheet terms that are present in (3) and (4). For brevity, we only describe in detail the manipulations necessary to obtain the shearing-sheet contributions to kinetic MHD, leaving the derivation of “standard” kinetic MHD terms out. The full derivation of kinetic MHD is involved, and has been presented in many prior works, such as Kulsrud (1964), Kulsrud (1983), and Kulsrud (2005); we encourage interested readers to consult these references.

Our starting point is the collisionless kinetic (Vlasov) equation for a particle species $s$ that represents either electrons or ions:

$$ \frac{\partial f_{s}}{\partial t}+\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,(\mbox{\boldmath{$v$}}f_{s})+\frac{\partial}{\partial\mbox{\boldmath{$v$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\left(\mbox{\boldmath{$a$}}_{s}(t,\mbox{\boldmath{$r$}},\mbox{\boldmath{$v$}})f_{s}\right)=0. $$

Here, $v$ represents the particles’ velocities and $\mbox{\boldmath{$a$}}_{s}$ their accelerations. Focusing exclusively on the forces unique to the local shearing-sheet approximation, the latter are provided by Hill’s equations (Hill, 1878; Goldreich & Lynden-Bell, 1965):

$$ a_{x,s}=-4\Omega_{0}A_{0}x+2\Omega_{0}v_{y}, a_{y,s}=-2\Omega_{0}v_{x}. $$

As in the main text, $x$ represents the local radial coordinates and $y$ represents the local azimuthal coordinate; $\mbox{\boldmath{$\Omega$}}(r_{0})=\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}$ is the rotation frequency and $A_{0}$ is Oort’s first constant. It is therefore implied that the $v$ are the particles’ velocities in the rotating frame described by (34). With the addition of magnetic ( $B$ ) and electric ( $E$ ) fields, the total acceleration appearing in (33) is then given by

$$ \mbox{\boldmath{$a$}}_{s}=\frac{q_{s}}{m_{s}}\left(\mbox{\boldmath{$E$}}+\frac{\mbox{\boldmath{$v$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}}{c}\right)-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\psi_{\rm eff}-2\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$v$}}, $$

where we have introduced the effective gravitational potential $\psi_{\rm eff}=2\Omega_{0}A_{0}x^{2}$ , the particle charges ( $q_{s}$ ) and masses ( $m_{s}$ ), and the speed of light ( $c$ ).

We now transform the Vlasov system to a frame that is co-moving with all bulk velocities (not just rotation), so that the resultant $f_{s}$ possesses no first-order velocity moment. This is accomplished by transforming from the total rotating-frame particle velocity $v$ to the peculiar velocities $\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}\equiv\mbox{\boldmath{$v$}}-\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}$ , where $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}=n_{s}^{-1}\int{\rm d}^{3}v\,\mbox{\boldmath{$v$}}f_{s}$ is the rotating-frame bulk-flow velocity and $n_{s}=\int{\rm d}^{3}v\,f_{s}$ is the number density. In this transformation, the time, space, and velocity gradients are modified according to

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rightarrow\frac{\partial}{\partial t}-\frac{\partial\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}}{\partial t}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}},\quad\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\rightarrow\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}-(\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s})\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}},\quad{\rm and}\quad\frac{\partial}{\partial\mbox{\boldmath{$v$}}}\rightarrow\frac{\partial}{\partial\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}}. $$

Substituting these derivatives and eliminating $v$ in favor of $\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}$ , we obtain

$$ \frac{{\rm d}f_{s}}{{\rm d}t_{s}}+\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}f_{s}+\left(\frac{q_{s}}{m_{s}}\frac{\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}}{c}-2\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}+\mbox{\boldmath{$a$}}_{s,\rm f}-\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}\right)\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\frac{\partial f_{s}}{\partial\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}}=0, $$

where ${\rm d}/{\rm d}t_{s}=\partial/\partial_{t}+\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}$ is the convective derivative for species $s$ and

$$ \mbox{\boldmath{$a$}}_{s,\rm f}=\frac{q_{s}}{m_{s}}\left(\mbox{\boldmath{$E$}}+\frac{\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}}{c}\right)-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\psi_{\rm eff}-2\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}-\frac{{\rm d}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}}{{\rm d}t_{s}} $$

is a collection of terms referred to as the “fluid” acceleration, for the fact that they do not depend on $\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}$ . Now, rather than the kinetic equation being one that is solved directly for $f_{s}$ from which $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}$ can be calculated, we have a system in which $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}$ is a field that must be determined separately so that $f_{s}$ can be evolved. It is therefore necessary to obtain an evolution equation for $\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}$ .

Taking the $m_{s}\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}$ moment of (37) (and noting that $\int{\rm d}^{3}w_{s}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}f_{s}=0$ by construction), the momentum equation is obtained:

$$ m_{s}n_{s}\frac{{\rm d}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}}{{\rm d}t_{s}}=-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\bm{\mathsf{P}}_{s}+q_{s}n_{s}\left(\mbox{\boldmath{$E$}}+\frac{\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}}{c}\right)-m_{s}n_{s}\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\psi_{\rm eff}-2\Omega_{0}m_{s}n_{s}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{s}. $$

Here $\bm{\mathsf{P}}_{s}=m_{s}\int{\rm d}^{3}w_{s}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}_{s}f_{s}$ is the pressure tensor for each species. From here, the standard MHD assumptions are applied, save for the assumption of LTE: quasi-neutrality ( $\sum q_{s}n_{s}=0$ ), negligible electron inertia ( $m_{\rm i}\gg m_{\rm e}$ ), long length scales ( $l\gg r_{\rm L}$ ), and long time scales ( $\omega\ll\omega_{\rm L}$ ). The outcome for the ion momentum equation is typical of MHD except for the presence of the shearing-sheet terms and the fact that the ion pressure remains anisotropic (as in §2, the electrons are taken to be cold and therefore make no contribution to the total thermal pressure):

$$ m_{i}n_{i}\frac{{\rm d}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{i}}{{\rm d}t_{i}}=-\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\bm{\mathsf{P}}_{i}-\frac{\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}B^{2}}{8\pi}+\frac{\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}}{4\pi}-m_{i}n_{i}\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\psi_{\rm eff}-2\Omega_{0}m_{i}n_{i}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{i}. $$

The resultant induction equation for $B$ is also standard:

$$ \frac{{\rm d}\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}}{{\rm d}t}=\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm i}-\mbox{\boldmath{$B$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}_{\rm i}. $$

There now exists a closed set of equations ((41), (40), and (37) with $s=\rm i$ ) that do not require any information about the (cold) electron distribution function. Henceforth, we drop all “i” subscript from the ion quantities.

Let us now return to the kinetic equation, where our remaining goal is to perform a gyro-average so that we may eliminate any dependence on the gyro-phase angle ( $\phi$ ) from our equations. For convenience, we first introduce an effective electric field,

$$ \mbox{\boldmath{$E$}}_{\rm eff}=\mbox{\boldmath{$E$}}-\frac{m}{e}\left(\mbox{\boldmath{$\nabla$}}\psi_{\rm eff}+2\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}\right), $$

which absorbs the “fluid” shearing-sheet terms into the standard electric field. Now, all of the remaining manipulations that apply to $E$ can be applied to $\mbox{\boldmath{$E$}}_{\rm eff}$ one-to-one. Consequently, the only new term that we need to gyro-average here is the peculiar Coriolis flux:

$$ F_{\rm C,p}\equiv-(2\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}})\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}}. $$

To make the gyro-averaging process easier, we first exchange the full peculiar velocity $w$ in favor of its magnitude ( $w$ ), its projection along $\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}$ ( $w_{\|}$ ), and the gyro-phase angle ( $\phi$ ). This transforms the $w$ derivative of $f$ into

$$ \frac{\partial f}{\partial\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}}\rightarrow\frac{\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}}{w}\frac{\partial f}{\partial w}+\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_{\|}}. $$

Applying this to $F_{\rm C,p}$ , we find that only the parallel gradient survives:

$$ F_{\rm C,p}=-2\Omega_{0}(\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}})\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\left(\frac{\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}}{w}\frac{\partial f}{\partial w}+\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_{\|}}\right)=-2\Omega_{0}(\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}})\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_{\|}}. $$

We now average this expression over the gyro-angle ( $\langle\rangle_{\phi}$ ), making use of the fact that the fast-gyrofrequency assumption ( $\omega\ll\omega_{\rm L,i}$ ) makes $f$ gyrotropic, and that $\left\langle{\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}}}\right\rangle_{\phi}=w_{\|}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}$ . The result is simply that $\langle F_{\rm C,p}\rangle_{\phi}=0$ because $\left\langle{(\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$w$}})\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}}\right\rangle_{\phi}=(\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,w_{\|}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}})\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}=0$ .

With $\langle F_{\rm C,p}\rangle_{\phi}=0$ , the remainder of the derivation is trivial. We take the standard drift-kinetic equation from kinetic MHD, and substitute $\mbox{\boldmath{$E$}}_{\rm eff}$ for the electric field to obtain

$$ \frac{{\rm D}f}{{\rm D}t}+\frac{{\rm D}\ln B}{{\rm D}t}\frac{w_{\perp}}{2}\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_{\perp}}-\biggl[\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\cdot$}}\,\biggl(\frac{{\rm D}\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}}{{\rm D}t}-\frac{e}{m}\mbox{\boldmath{$E$}}+2\Omega_{0}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$z$}}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$\times$}}\,\mbox{\boldmath{$u$}}+4A_{0}\Omega_{0}x\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$x$}}}\biggr)+\frac{w_{\perp}^{2}}{2}\nabla_{\|}\ln B\biggr]\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_{\|}}=0. $$

One final technical detail concerns the ion pressure tensor $\bm{\mathsf{P}}_{\rm i}$ . Because $\left\langle{\mbox{\boldmath{$ww$}}}\right\rangle_{\phi}=(w_{\perp}^{2}/2)(\bm{\mathsf{I}}-\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}})+w_{\|}^{2}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}$ , the pressure tensor for a gyrotropic distribution is simply $\bm{\mathsf{P}}=p_{\perp}(\bm{\mathsf{I}}-\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}})+p_{\|}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}\hat{\mbox{\boldmath{$b$}}}$ . With this simplification, the momentum equation (40) becomes exactly that which we use in the main text.

## Abstract

A theory of cosmic-ray transport in multi-phase diffusive media is developed, with the specific application to cases in which the cosmic-ray diffusion coefficient has large spatial fluctuations that may be inherently multi-scale. We demonstrate that the resulting transport of cosmic rays is diffusive in the long-time limit, with an average diffusion coefficient equal to the harmonic mean of the spatially varying diffusion coefficient. Thus, cosmic-ray transport is dominated by areas of low diffusion even if these areas occupy a relatively small, but not infinitesimal, fraction of the volume. On intermediate time scales, the cosmic rays experience transient effective sub-diffusion, as a result of low-diffusion regions interrupting long flights through high-diffusion regions. In the simplified case of a two-phase medium, we show that the extent and extremity of the sub-diffusivity of cosmic-ray transport is controlled by the spectral exponent of the distribution of patch sizes of each of the phases. We finally show that, despite strongly influencing the confinement times, the multi-phase medium is only capable of altering the energy dependence of cosmic-ray transport when there is a moderate (but not excessive) level of perpendicular diffusion across magnetic-field lines.

#### Keywords:

## 1 Introduction

*Figure 1: Cartoon of a patchy two-phase medium. In the left panel, the two-phase medium is depicted with regions of high parallel-diffusion coefficient in white and regions of low parallel-diffusion coefficient shaded in blue. CRs are sourced in localised areas of space, shown in red, across multiple field lines. The magnetic-field lines threading the media, to which CRs would be tied, are shown as black lines. The patchy stochastic structure is multi-scale, meaning that the distributions of patch lengths along magnetic-field lines, shown in the upper right panel, will typically be power laws. From these distributions, $P_{\mathrm{high}}(l)$ for high-diffusion patches and $P_{\mathrm{low}}(l)$ for low-diffusion patches, a single realisation of the spatially varying diffusion coefficient $\kappa(x)$ along a magnetic-field line can be constructed and is shown in the lower right panel.*

The transport of cosmic rays (CRs), particularly low-energy ( ${\sim\!1\!-\!100\,\mathrm{GeV}}$ ) CRs, has major implications for the launching of galactic winds (e.g., Ruszkowski et al. 2017; Quataert et al. 2022a; Quataert et al. 2022b), cosmological structure formation and galactic feedback (e.g., Hopkins et al. 2020; Quataert & Hopkins 2025), re-ionisation in the early Universe (e.g., Farcy et al. 2025), the morphology of the circumgalactic medium (e.g., Faucher-Giguère & Oh 2023; Weber et al. 2025), and much more besides (see, e.g., Ruszkowski & Pfrommer 2023 and references therein). In each of these situations, a common feature is that the CRs propagate not through a homogeneous medium with constant scattering rates but through a patchy, usually turbulent, environment that is frequently composed of multiple regions with distinct material properties. Indeed it has been convincingly proposed that an intermittent picture of CR transport (Kempski et al. 2023; Lemoine 2023; Butsky et al. 2024) is required to resolve basic discrepancies between standard scattering models and CR observables (Kempski & Quataert 2022; Hopkins et al. 2022c). The multi-phase nature of the medium may arise from macroscopically distinct fluid environments (e.g., Sameer et al. 2024; Beattie et al. 2025; Hu 2025) or microphysical differences caused by turbulence in the underlying fluid (e.g., Squire et al. 2021; Hopkins et al. 2022b; Kempski et al. 2023; Lemoine 2023; Reichherzer et al. 2025b). The extreme diversity of such multi-phase environments naturally prompts two fundamental questions:

- • For a given multi-phase medium, with each phase having a prescribed CR transport mechanism (ballistic streaming, diffusion, etc.), what are the average transport properties of the medium—in brief, what is the ‘mean-field’ model of the medium?

- • What features of the multi-phase medium (e.g., filling fraction, topology, intermittency, etc.) impact the mean-field theory most?

In this paper, we answer these questions for a particularly simple model of CR transport. We consider the CRs to be tied to magnetic-field lines with a small diffusion coefficient perpendicular to the field, and assume that, while travelling along a single magnetic-field line, the CRs experience a spatially varying diffusion coefficient.11 1 This is, effectively, a complementary set-up to that investigated by Butsky et al. (2024), in that both studies consider diffusion due to patchy substructure. We consider a population of CRs experiencing continuous diffusion over a large volume while confined to a 1D magnetic field, while Butsky et al. (2024) considered CRs experiencing ballistic motion interrupted by events of extreme scattering that occupy a small fraction of the volume. In a separate paper (Reichherzer et al. 2025a), we consider the case in which this spatially varying diffusion coefficient arises from regions of fluid turbulence that are unstable to micro-scale plasma instabilities (Schekochihin et al. 2005; Squire et al. 2023; Majeski et al. 2024; Bott et al. 2024), which alter the local transport properties of CRs (Ewart et al. 2024; Reichherzer et al. 2025b). In this paper, in pursuit of the general questions posed above, we are agnostic towards the microphysics of diffusion: the Universe has provided a multi-phase medium and it is the CRs’ manifest destiny to propagate through it; the question is how they do so.

The central results, and outline of this paper, are as follows. In Section 2, we first consider the mean-field theory. Naturally, on short length scales (equivalently, on short time scales), the transport is diffusive. This arises simply because CRs do not initially ‘know’ that they are in a multi-phase medium—they experience only the diffusion coefficient characteristic of their local patch of space. If every CR initially knows only its local diffusion coefficient, then the effective diffusion coefficient is the spatially averaged diffusion coefficient of the system. On larger length scales (longer times) the transport is made more complicated by the fact that CRs will have sampled several different ‘patches’ of the multi-phase medium. We show that, asymptotically, after the CRs have sampled many patches, their transport will again be diffusive but with an effective diffusion coefficient set by the harmonic mean of the local diffusion coefficient—an exact result (at late times), which we present in Section 2 (the proof is given in Appendix B). This means that the diffusive transport of CRs along magnetic-field lines is most sensitive to the areas having the smallest diffusion coefficients.

Thus, in a system where the local diffusion coefficient varies greatly, and over many length scales, the details of the transport naturally become sensitive to the nature of the spatial variation. In particular, since the CRs are diffusive at short times and diffusive again at large times, but with a smaller effective diffusion coefficient (since the harmonic mean is always smaller than the arithmetic mean), they must experience a transient period of sub-diffusion at intermediate times (cf. Liang & Oh 2025). This transient period is, naturally, a function of how long a CR can diffuse uninterrupted before fully sampling the multi-phase medium. The nature of the transport is therefore controlled by the sizes of the patches in the multi-phase medium, which are likely to be randomly distributed. As a model for such random multi-phase structure, which we refer to as ‘stochastic inhomogeneity’, we consider the cartoon set-up shown in Figure 1: magnetic-field lines thread a two-phase multi-scale medium, and the patch lengths have a power-law distribution along a magnetic-field line. In Section 3, we present a heuristic description of (and semi-analytic expression for) the resulting transient sub-diffusivity. We show that the predictions of this description are in robust agreement with numerical Monte-Carlo simulations of inhomogeneous diffusion equations. Despite the fact that the multi-scale, multi-phase nature of the medium can drastically alter the magnitude of the CR transport coefficient, we argue in Section 3.2 (in the case of purely parallel diffusion) that the medium does not imprint its structure on the energy dependence of the CR transport (i.e., stochastic inhomogeneities affect the prefactor of the CR escape rate, but not its energy scaling). This is simply because the 1D geometry of parallel diffusion greatly constrains the path that CRs can take through the medium: they must tackle every low-diffusion patch head on. When a small amount of perpendicular diffusion is allowed, CRs instead navigate diffusively around the low-diffusion zones. If both the parallel and perpendicular diffusion coefficients are functions of the CR energy, then we should expect that the navigability of the medium will become a function of the CR energy. In Section 4, we present a heuristic description of the effect that this circumnavigation has on transport, arguing that, in the case of moderate (but not extreme) perpendicular diffusion, the stochastic inhomogeneity of the multi-phase medium can imprint itself on the energy dependence of the CR diffusivity. In Section 5, we summarise our progress and discuss future avenues of research.

## 2 Theory
